days.title: Platform Architecture: Control and Compute Planes, Delta Lake, Unity Catalog and Choosing Compute

concepts.heading: Control Plane and Compute Plane
concepts.body: A Databricks workspace is split in two. The control plane is managed by Databricks and holds the web application, the notebook and job services, cluster management and workspace metadata. The compute plane is where data is actually processed. With classic compute the compute plane lives in the customer's own cloud account, so clusters start as VMs there and read data over the customer's network and storage. With serverless compute the resources run in a serverless compute plane in the Databricks account, and the engineer configures no instances at all. This split explains many design choices: classic compute gives control over instance types, networking and runtime, while serverless trades that control for no infrastructure work and fast start-up. A useful mental walk-through: you press Run on a job in the Jobs UI, the request goes to the control plane, and the control plane launches the compute that executes the Spark tasks in the compute plane. Exam questions about where something runs always come back to this two-plane picture.

concepts.heading: Delta Lake: Parquet Files Plus a Transaction Log
concepts.body: Delta Lake is the default table format on Databricks: if you create a table without naming a format, it is a Delta table. Its data files are ordinary Parquet, but the table is defined by the transaction log in the _delta_log folder, which records every commit as an ordered list of actions such as add this file or remove that file. Readers rebuild the table from the log, never by listing files. That is what gives ACID guarantees. A write first creates new data files that belong to no table version, and they become visible only when the commit entry is added to the log atomically. If a job dies halfway, for example with an out-of-memory error after writing some files, the files stay orphaned, readers never see them, and VACUUM removes them later. The same log provides scalable metadata handling and the history used for time travel. Formats such as plain Parquet or CSV tables lack the log and therefore lack these guarantees.

concepts.heading: Time Travel, RESTORE and Retention
concepts.body: Every commit adds a numbered version to the log. DESCRIBE HISTORY lists versions with timestamp, user, operation and metrics. Time travel reads an old state without changing the table: `SELECT * FROM orders VERSION AS OF 14` or `TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-10-30'`. RESTORE goes further and makes the table itself equal to an old version: `RESTORE TABLE orders TO VERSION AS OF 14`. The restore is a new commit, so history stays intact, and it needs MODIFY permission. Both depend on the old data files still existing, and two retention settings matter. The log is kept for logRetentionDuration (30 days by default), which is what DESCRIBE HISTORY shows, while the data files of old versions are kept for deletedFileRetentionDuration (7 days by default) and VACUUM deletes unreferenced files older than that. So a version can appear in the history while its files are already gone and the query fails. History is not an archive: for longer time travel raise both properties, accepting more storage, or keep a separate copy.

concepts.heading: Unity Catalog: One Governance Layer
concepts.body: Unity Catalog is the governance layer for data and AI across workspaces. It gives centralized access control, lineage, auditing and data discovery, so an administrator defines who can read a table once and every workspace attached to the metastore enforces it. Securable objects follow a three-level namespace, catalog.schema.object. The catalog is the top container, often one per environment or domain such as dev and prod. The schema groups tables, views, volumes and functions. The object is the table, view, volume or function itself. A table is therefore addressed as `prod.crm.customers`, and the metastore above the catalogs is attached to workspaces but is not typed in the name. Privileges are granted on these objects and inherit downward, for example `GRANT SELECT ON TABLE prod.crm.customers TO analysts`. Keep the roles apart: Delta Lake defines how a table stores data, Unity Catalog defines who may use it, and compute executes the queries and enforces what Unity Catalog decided.

concepts.heading: Choosing Compute for the Workload
concepts.body: Pick compute by workload shape. All-purpose compute is for interactive notebook work: it is shared, stays up until it auto-terminates and is billed at the interactive rate, so setting automatic termination removes idle cost, whereas autoscaling alone does not stop an idle cluster. Job compute is created for one job run and ends with it, which suits a nightly ETL notebook far better than a shared cluster. Serverless compute for jobs and notebooks needs no configuration and scales by itself, which fits variable volumes, but it has documented limits, for example only Spark Connect APIs work, so RDD calls such as `sc.parallelize` fail and must be rewritten with DataFrames. A SQL warehouse is the compute for SQL queries, dashboards and BI tools, and serverless SQL warehouses are recommended because they start quickly and scale with concurrency. Single node compute has a driver and no workers and is meant for small data or non-distributed libraries. SQL tasks in a job use a SQL warehouse.

examPoints: A question about where the web application and where Spark executes differ is testing the control plane (Databricks managed) versus the compute plane (customer account for classic, Databricks account for serverless).

A question about a failed write that leaves partial files, or an old version that can no longer be read, is testing the transaction log: commits are atomic, and time travel depends on files that VACUUM has not yet removed.

A question that picks compute for nightly ETL, BI dashboards, tiny single-library work or RDD code is testing job or serverless compute, serverless SQL warehouse, single node, and the serverless limitation to Spark Connect APIs.

quiz.q: A team's weekly report job reads `TIMESTAMP AS OF` a date 20 days ago on a table that is vacuumed with default settings and whose properties were never changed. DESCRIBE HISTORY lists that date, yet the query fails. What is the most likely reason?
choices: Time travel works only for versions created by MERGE, and that date belongs to an append operation that cannot be read back
The log entries remain for much longer than the data files, and the files of that version were already removed by VACUUM
The table must first be converted from Parquet to Delta, because only Delta tables written by Unity Catalog jobs support timestamps
The transaction log was truncated automatically, so the history listing shows entries that were copied from a backup of the table
quiz.explain: The log is kept 30 days by default while the data files of old versions are kept 7 days by default, so a listed version can have no files left. The first choice sounds plausible but time travel is independent of the operation type.

quiz.q: A nightly pipeline written with `rdd = sc.parallelize(rows).map(parse)` runs on a classic job cluster. The team moves it to serverless compute for jobs and it fails with an unsupported operation error, while a sibling pipeline written with DataFrames runs unchanged. What should the team do?
choices: Increase the instance size of the serverless compute, because the RDD operation needs more driver memory than the default
Enable the Spark Context option in the job settings, which allows RDD operations on serverless compute for approved users
Move the job to a SQL warehouse, because warehouses support all Spark APIs including RDDs for scheduled tasks
Rewrite the logic with DataFrame or SQL APIs, or stay on classic compute, because serverless supports only Spark Connect APIs
quiz.explain: Serverless compute supports only Spark Connect APIs, so RDD code must be rewritten or stay on classic compute. Serverless has no instance size to raise and a SQL warehouse runs SQL, not RDD code.

days.recap: Databricks splits a Databricks-managed control plane from a compute plane (customer account for classic, Databricks account for serverless). Delta Lake is Parquet plus a transaction log (ACID, time travel, RESTORE, 7-day file versus 30-day log retention). Unity Catalog governs catalog.schema.object across workspaces. Match compute to the workload.

days.title: Ingestion Patterns and COPY INTO: Batch, Streaming, Incremental Batch and Idempotent File Loads

concepts.heading: Batch, Streaming and Incremental Batch
concepts.body: Three patterns cover most ingestion. Batch reads a fixed input and finishes; run again on a growing folder it re-reads everything unless you track what was already processed. Streaming keeps a query running and processes data as it arrives. Incremental batch is the middle path: a scheduled run processes only what is new since the last run and then stops. In Structured Streaming that is `trigger(availableNow=True)`, which consumes everything available when the run starts, possibly in several micro-batches, and shuts down. The freshness requirement picks the pattern. If data may be hours old, a scheduled incremental run is cheapest because compute exists only while it runs. If the target is a minute or seconds, the query must run continuously with a trigger interval such as `processingTime='1 minute'`. A shorter interval lowers latency; a longer one reduces checks and small files. Example: JSON files land hourly in a volume and must reach bronze within a few hours, so run Auto Loader with availableNow on a schedule.

concepts.heading: Triggers: availableNow Instead of once
concepts.body: A trigger decides when a streaming query runs micro-batches. The default and `processingTime` run continuously, checking for new data on the interval. `availableNow=True` processes all data available at start and then stops; options such as `maxBytesPerTrigger` still apply, so a large backlog is split into manageable batches. The older `once=True` ran a single micro-batch over everything available and is deprecated; Databricks recommends availableNow for all incremental batch workloads, and serverless notebooks and jobs support only availableNow (and the deprecated once), not processingTime. When a reviewer asks to move off trigger once, the answer is availableNow. Progress is remembered in the checkpoint, which is why a stopped query can start later and continue where it ended. The write side looks like `df.writeStream.option('checkpointLocation', chk).trigger(availableNow=True).toTable('main.bronze.events')`. Each streaming query needs its own checkpoint location.

concepts.heading: Tables and Files as Incremental Sources
concepts.body: Incremental does not only apply to files. A Delta table can be a streaming source: `spark.readStream.table('main.bronze.orders')` remembers in the checkpoint which table versions were already processed, so each run reads only rows appended since the last one. Combined with availableNow this gives incremental batch between layers with exactly-once behavior. By contrast, `spark.read.table` is a batch read that returns the table as it is now, and time travel with versionAsOf reads one fixed historic version without tracking progress. For files in cloud storage or a volume, Auto Loader (the cloudFiles source) records the files it has seen in the checkpoint. It adds scalable discovery, schema inference and evolution, and a rescued data column compared with the plain file source. It guarantees exactly-once processing of files but not their order, so an upsert should compare an update timestamp before overwriting a newer target row, and deletes are safer as soft deletes.

concepts.heading: COPY INTO: Idempotent SQL File Loads
concepts.body: COPY INTO is a retriable, idempotent SQL command that loads files into a Delta table. It records which files were loaded for the target, and on later runs skips them by default (the `force` copy option is false), so a statement that timed out after half the files can simply be rerun and loads only the rest. Tracking is by file, not by row, so two different files with the same rows would both load. A typical statement: `COPY INTO main.bronze.sales FROM 's3://acme-raw/sales/' FILEFORMAT = CSV FORMAT_OPTIONS ('header' = 'true')`. FORMAT_OPTIONS hold file-reader settings while COPY_OPTIONS hold copy behavior. Reading the path needs permission: define it as an external location in Unity Catalog and hold READ FILES on it, since MODIFY on the target only controls writing. It fits modest file counts. For a more scalable and robust SQL experience, Databricks recommends streaming tables, which use Auto Loader underneath.

concepts.heading: COPY INTO Options That Decide Exam Answers
concepts.body: Know the options by purpose. A file that was rewritten in place with the same name is skipped even if modified; to reload it set `COPY_OPTIONS ('force' = 'true')`, restrict the selection because force applies to every selected file, and remove the old rows first or the target holds both versions. FILES takes an explicit list of literal names while PATTERN takes a glob, and the two cannot be combined; with thousands of matching files use PATTERN. VALIDATE makes a dry run that checks parsing, schema match, nullability and constraints without writing, and `VALIDATE 15 ROWS` checks a sample; remove it to load. To let the target schema evolve, set `mergeSchema` to true in COPY_OPTIONS and, when the schema comes from the files, in FORMAT_OPTIONS too. An empty placeholder table without columns can be filled this way, but until the first load INSERT INTO and MERGE are not supported on it. Concurrent statements are allowed only on distinct file sets, and one statement over many files beats many single-file statements.

examPoints: A question that asks for processing only new data on a schedule with no always-on cluster is testing incremental batch with availableNow, and a request to replace trigger once is testing that availableNow is the recommended trigger.
A question about rerunning a COPY INTO after a timeout, or about a corrected file that was not reloaded, is testing idempotency by file and the force copy option.
A question on checking a vendor file without writing rows, adding a new column automatically or selecting files by wildcard is testing VALIDATE, mergeSchema and PATTERN, in that order.

quiz.q: A gold refresh job must read, on each hourly run, only the rows added since the previous run to the append-only table main.silver.payments, then stop so the cluster can terminate. Which design does that?
choices: Read main.silver.payments with spark.readStream.table, write with a checkpoint location and trigger(availableNow=True)
Read main.silver.payments with spark.read.table and filter on the current hour, since batch reads remember processed versions
Read the table with VERSION AS OF set to the last known version and rewrite that version again each hour
Run COPY INTO from the table path into the target, because COPY INTO tracks which Delta versions were loaded
quiz.explain: A Delta table read as a stream remembers processed versions in the checkpoint, and availableNow stops the query afterward. COPY INTO loads from files, not from another table, and a batch read has no memory of earlier runs.

quiz.q: A COPY INTO statement scheduled every night loads CSV files from a landing folder. One night it fails after loading most files because the cluster was preempted. What should the team do to finish the load safely?
choices: Delete the target table and rerun the statement with force enabled so every file is loaded in one clean pass
Rerun the same statement, because files already loaded are skipped and only the remaining files are loaded
Add the VALIDATE clause to the statement, because validation repairs the file tracking after a failed run
Run the statement again with mergeSchema enabled so that already loaded files are matched against the target
quiz.explain: COPY INTO is idempotent per file, so a plain rerun loads only the files not yet loaded. Force would reload everything and duplicate rows, and VALIDATE is a dry run that writes nothing.

days.recap: Pick the pattern by freshness: batch, continuous streaming or incremental batch with availableNow (once is deprecated). Delta tables and Auto Loader both track progress in a checkpoint. COPY INTO is idempotent per file, with force, VALIDATE, PATTERN and mergeSchema as the key options; streaming tables are the scalable SQL step up.

days.title: Auto Loader: File Detection Modes, Schema Inference and Evolution, Rescued Data and Checkpoints

concepts.heading: Directory Listing versus File Notification
concepts.body: Auto Loader discovers new files in one of two modes. Directory listing is the default: it lists the input directory, starts quickly and needs only storage access. With a continuous trigger it re-lists the directory on every interval, so when millions of files accumulate, LIST calls dominate cost and discovery slows down. File notification subscribes to file events and reads them from a queue instead of listing. The recommended form uses file events on a Unity Catalog external location: one queue per location serves all streams, no extra credentials are needed per stream, and discovery is incremental. It is enabled with `cloudFiles.useManagedFileEvents`. Both modes give exactly-once processing and you can switch between them across restarts. If file events cannot be enabled and processed files pile up, `cloudFiles.cleanSource` can MOVE files to an archive (the destination must be in the same external location or volume) or DELETE them, optionally after a retention duration, so fewer files are listed. That option changes the source folder, so check that no other consumer needs the files there.

concepts.heading: schemaLocation and Inferred Types
concepts.body: A basic Auto Loader stream is `spark.readStream.format('cloudFiles').option('cloudFiles.format','json').option('cloudFiles.schemaLocation', chk).load(path)`. Setting `cloudFiles.schemaLocation` turns on schema inference and evolution: Auto Loader samples the first 50 GB or 1000 files, whichever limit is crossed first, infers the schema and stores it, with every later change, in a _schemas directory there. The directory can be the same as the checkpoint location, which is the writer option that tracks progress, not the schema store. Without a schema location, inference has nowhere to keep the schema and the stream fails at start. For formats that do not encode types (JSON, CSV, XML) all columns are inferred as strings, including nested JSON fields, which avoids evolution problems from type mismatches. Parquet and Avro keep their encoded types. To get Spark-style inference set `cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes` to true, or fix particular columns with `cloudFiles.schemaHints`, for example `'amount DOUBLE, ts TIMESTAMP'`.

concepts.heading: Schema Evolution Modes
concepts.body: When producers add columns, `cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode` decides what happens. The default without a provided schema is addNewColumns: Auto Loader infers the schema of the latest micro-batch, merges the new columns at the end of the schema while existing types stay unchanged, and then the stream stops with UnknownFieldException. Restarting resumes with the updated schema, which is why Databricks recommends running such streams in Lakeflow Jobs with automatic retry so they restart by themselves. The rescue mode never evolves the schema and never fails because of schema changes; new columns go to the rescued data column. failOnNewColumns fails and keeps failing until you update the schema or remove the file. none does not evolve, ignores new columns, does not fail, and rescues nothing unless the rescued data column is set. A compliance rule such as the table schema must never change automatically and the stream must never fail, yet new values must stay available, points to rescue. A schema fixed by hints or a provided schema is enforced the same way.

concepts.heading: The Rescued Data Column
concepts.body: Auto Loader adds the column `_rescued_data` to an inferred schema. It receives data that could not be parsed into the schema: a column missing from the schema, a type mismatch, or a name that differs only in case. The value is a JSON blob holding the rescued values and the source file path. With the rescued data column active, a type mismatch does not drop the record in DROPMALFORMED mode or fail it in FAILFAST mode; only truly corrupt records such as malformed JSON or CSV are treated as bad. Example: the schema says age INT but a record carries 'age': 'N/A'. The row is kept, age is NULL, and 'N/A' appears in _rescued_data. Downstream you can inspect, alert on, or reprocess rescued values instead of losing them. This is the practical meaning of schema enforcement in a bronze layer: the declared schema is applied, nothing is silently dropped, and mismatches are visible in one place.

concepts.heading: Checkpoints and One Stream per Checkpoint
concepts.body: The checkpoint holds offsets, commits, state and the query ID. For Auto Loader, metadata of discovered files lives in a RocksDB store in the checkpoint location, which gives exactly-once file processing and lets a failed stream resume where it stopped. If the checkpoint is deleted or the job points to a new location, the next run starts fresh; cloudFiles.includeExistingFiles (default true) is evaluated on the first start, so every historic file is loaded again and the target gets duplicates. Treat the checkpoint as part of the table's state and change it only on purpose, for example for a full backfill with target truncation. Each streaming query must own its checkpoint: two Auto Loader streams reading /landing/orders and /landing/returns into one bronze table still need two checkpoint locations, since a shared one mixes offsets and can lose or duplicate data. Combined with availableNow, the checkpoint is also what makes a scheduled run incremental.

examPoints: A question about LIST cost growing with a continuous trigger, or slow discovery with millions of processed files, is testing file notification with file events, and cleanSource when events are unavailable.

A question about a stream that fails at start without options, columns arriving as strings, or a stream that stops once when a column is added is testing schemaLocation, inferColumnTypes or schemaHints, and addNewColumns with restart in Lakeflow Jobs.

A question that must keep bad or new values without failing is testing the rescued data column and the rescue mode, and a question about duplicated history after a refactor is testing a replaced checkpoint.

quiz.q: A bronze Auto Loader stream reads JSON order files. The stream is declared with schemaEvolutionMode set to addNewColumns. A producer adds a field loyalty_tier. What does the team observe, and what is the recommended operating practice?
choices: The new field is silently dropped and the stream keeps running, so the team must read the field from the source files directly
The stream restarts itself in the same run and the new column appears at the front of the table with all existing types converted to strings
The stream stops once with UnknownFieldException, then continues after a restart with the new column, so Lakeflow Jobs with retry automates it
The stream fails permanently until an engineer deletes the schema location, because addNewColumns cannot evolve an existing schema
quiz.explain: addNewColumns updates the stored schema, stops the stream once, and the restart resumes with the merged schema; jobs with retry handle the restart. Dropping new fields silently describes mode none, and permanent failure describes failOnNewColumns.

quiz.q: Two ingestion pipelines are written by different teams. One Auto Loader stream reads s3://acme/landing/clicks and another reads s3://acme/landing/views, and both write to the same bronze table. To save setup, a developer proposes giving both streams the same checkpointLocation. What is the correct approach?
choices: Share the checkpoint, because both streams write to the same target table and the table defines the progress
Share the checkpoint but give the streams different schema locations so that their inferred schemas stay separate
Use one checkpoint only for the stream with more files and let the smaller stream run without any checkpoint
Give each stream its own checkpoint location, because a checkpoint holds the offsets and file state of one query only
quiz.explain: Each streaming query needs its own checkpoint, even when the target is the same table, because offsets and discovered-file state belong to one query. Sharing mixes progress and can lose or duplicate data.

days.recap: Auto Loader finds files by directory listing or file notification (file events preferred at scale). schemaLocation enables inference and evolution; JSON and CSV columns default to strings unless inferColumnTypes or hints are set. addNewColumns stops once then continues, rescue never fails, _rescued_data keeps mismatches. One checkpoint per stream.

days.title: Lakeflow Connect and Programmatic Ingestion: Managed and Standard Connectors, JDBC, ODBC and REST Sources

concepts.heading: The Lakeflow Connect Connector Families
concepts.body: Lakeflow Connect ingests from files, enterprise applications, databases, cloud storage and message buses, in layers from most managed to most customizable. Fully-managed connectors are built and run by Databricks for popular SaaS applications such as Salesforce and databases such as SQL Server. They build on Lakeflow pipelines and add source-specific authentication, change data capture or cursor handling, automated retries and schema evolution. The more customizable layer is Lakeflow pipelines and Structured Streaming, which you configure yourself with SQL and Spark APIs: Auto Loader and streaming tables for files in cloud storage or volumes, and streaming sources for message buses such as Kafka. The overview never says standard connectors; read the term in exam wording as this self-configured layer, set against the managed one. Release states differ by connector, so check a connector's page before relying on it. Databricks recommends starting with the most managed layer and dropping down only when it cannot satisfy the requirement, for example an unsupported source. Example: Salesforce data with incremental refresh and little code means a managed connector, while a folder of CSV files means Auto Loader.

concepts.heading: Anatomy of a Managed Connector
concepts.body: A managed connector is built from Unity Catalog governed pieces. A connection is a securable object that stores the authentication details for the source, so credentials never appear in the pipeline definition, and access to it is controlled with Unity Catalog privileges. An ingestion pipeline is a Lakeflow pipeline that reads from the source and writes to the destination, and destination tables are streaming tables that hold the ingested data. Database connectors that use change data capture add an ingestion gateway and staging storage. The gateway runs in its own job as a continuous task, extracting change data and staging it, while the scheduled pipeline applies the staged changes to the streaming tables. Example: a SQL Server table changes all day, the gateway keeps reading the change feed, and a pipeline run every hour applies it. Connections can also be created programmatically, for example with the Connections API or the Databricks CLI, so setup can be scripted.

concepts.heading: Scheduling, Incremental Runs and Recovery
concepts.body: You can run a managed ingestion pipeline on one or more custom schedules. For every schedule you add, Lakeflow Connect creates a Lakeflow Jobs job in which the ingestion pipeline is a task. You can add more tasks to that job, so a notebook that refreshes a silver table can depend on the ingestion task and start only after it succeeds, with retries and notifications available like any job. On the first run a connector ingests all selected data and in parallel tracks changes; later runs ingest only what changed since the prior run when the source supports it. The mechanism depends on the source: SQL Server offers change tracking and CDC, while Salesforce selects a cursor column. Sources or tables without support are read in full. When a connector fails it retries automatically with exponential backoff. Errors needing a person, such as expired credentials, do not lose data: the stored cursor position lets the next run continue from where it stopped. Pipelines can be deployed across environments with Declarative Automation Bundles.

concepts.heading: JDBC and ODBC Ingestion Done Right
concepts.body: When no connector fits, Spark can read a database over JDBC. By default `spark.read.format('jdbc')` with only url, dbtable and credentials reads the table with one query on one task, however large the cluster. For parallel reads set four options together: partitionColumn (a numeric, date or timestamp column, ideally indexed and evenly distributed), lowerBound, upperBound and numPartitions. Spark then issues one range query per partition. The bounds only compute the stride, they do not filter: the first partition takes everything below the first boundary and the last everything above the last, so a read with bounds 1000 to 2000 still returns the entire table. To load a subset, pass a parenthesized subquery with an alias as dbtable, which also pushes joins and aggregations to the source so that only the reduced result crosses the network, at the price of running work on a source that may serve an application. Keep numPartitions modest so the database is not overwhelmed. Databricks recommends Lakehouse Federation instead when it supports the source, and its JDBC page is marked experimental. Keep credentials in a secret scope and read them with `dbutils.secrets.get`.

concepts.heading: REST APIs, Client Libraries and Lakeflow Jobs
concepts.body: Auto Loader, COPY INTO and managed database connectors do not call arbitrary REST endpoints. The usual pattern is code orchestrated by Lakeflow Jobs: a Python or notebook task calls the API with an HTTP client such as `requests`, handles pagination and retries, and writes the responses to a Delta table. Keeping the raw JSON string in bronze preserves the source exactly and lets a downstream task parse and fix types later, so a nightly job might chain a pull_api task and a parse_to_silver task. The API token belongs in a secret scope, read with `dbutils.secrets.get('scope','key')`, and the value is redacted in notebook output. In the other direction, an application outside Databricks can use the Databricks JDBC driver, the ODBC driver or the Databricks SQL Connector for Python to run SQL on a SQL warehouse or all-purpose compute. Inserting a few thousand rows with `cursor.executemany` is fine; larger volumes are better written as files to cloud storage or a volume and ingested incrementally with Auto Loader or COPY INTO.

examPoints: A question that wants Salesforce or SQL Server data with automatic retries, schema evolution and minimal code is testing the fully-managed layer, and a question about where source credentials live is testing the Unity Catalog connection.
A question about chaining a notebook after a managed pipeline is testing that Lakeflow Connect creates a Lakeflow Jobs job per schedule, to which you add dependent tasks.
A question on a slow or oversized JDBC read is testing the four partitioning options and that bounds do not filter, while a REST API source is testing Lakeflow Jobs code plus a secret scope.

quiz.q: A data engineer reads a 400-million-row customers table from MySQL with `spark.read.format('jdbc')` and sets partitionColumn=customer_id, lowerBound=5000000, upperBound=6000000, numPartitions=8, expecting a one-million-row extract. The job returns all 400 million rows. What explains the result, and how is the extract limited?
choices: Spark ignores the bounds when the table has an index; the engineer must remove the partitionColumn option to enable filtering
The bounds only set the partition stride, so rows outside them land in the first and last partitions; use a filtered subquery as dbtable
The numPartitions value is too low to apply the bounds; increasing it to at least the number of rows per stride enforces the range
The JDBC source applies the bounds only after the data was written to Delta, so a later DELETE statement must remove the surplus rows
quiz.explain: lowerBound and upperBound only compute the stride; the first and last partitions take everything outside them. Restrict rows with a parenthesized subquery or a pushed-down filter. The other choices invent behavior for indexes and partition counts.

quiz.q: A managed Salesforce connector pipeline runs daily. After each successful run a notebook must rebuild a silver table, and a failure of the notebook should be retried without rerunning ingestion. What is the recommended setup?
choices: Add the notebook as a task of the job that Lakeflow Connect created for the schedule, depending on the ingestion task
Schedule the notebook separately at a fixed time later in the morning and hope the ingestion has finished by then
Call the notebook from inside the ingestion pipeline definition, because managed connectors allow custom code in each flow
Replace the managed connector by a REST pull in the notebook, because connectors cannot be combined with other tasks
quiz.explain: Each schedule creates a Lakeflow Jobs job with the pipeline as a task, so a dependent notebook task and its retries are ordinary job features. A separate fixed-time schedule has no dependency and managed pipelines do not embed custom notebooks.

days.recap: Start with the most managed Lakeflow Connect layer: managed connectors use a Unity Catalog connection, an ingestion pipeline and streaming tables (plus gateway and staging for CDC databases). The self-configured (standard) layer is Auto Loader, streaming tables and streaming sources. JDBC needs partition options and bounds do not filter; REST needs job code and secrets.

days.title: Choosing an Ingestion Method, Semi-Structured and Unstructured Data, and Domain 2 Review

concepts.heading: Choosing by Source, Volume and Freshness
concepts.body: Choose the method from the requirement, not from habit. Databricks recommends ingestion for most use cases because it scales to high volumes, supports low-latency queries and respects third-party API limits; the cost is a copy that can go stale. Query in place with Lakehouse Federation, which exposes an external relational database as a Unity Catalog foreign catalog with pushed-down, read-only, per-table governed queries, fits occasional look-ups, BI proofs of concept and cases where copying is not wanted yet. Recurring files in cloud storage or a volume call for Auto Loader, COPY INTO or a streaming table. Databases and SaaS applications call for managed connectors with scheduled or continuous incremental refresh. Message buses and event streams call for streaming connectors and Structured Streaming. A single small one-off file, such as a 20 MB budget CSV on a laptop, is simply uploaded through the add-data UI to create a table with no pipeline and no code. A method that is too heavy for the need is as wrong as one that is too light.

concepts.heading: When No Managed Connector Exists
concepts.body: Work down the layers. First the fully-managed connectors. If the source is not covered, community connectors are open-source connectors built and maintained by the community for sources without managed support; you can use one that is already registered, but it is not backed by Databricks SLAs. If none exists, a custom connector is one you build, test, deploy and run yourself in your own workspace, without registering it, and the result can still land in Unity Catalog governed tables. Validated ingestion partners are third-party tools that Databricks has validated, some reachable through Partner Connect; they suit organizations that already license the tool or sources it covers better than a managed connector, and configuration varies by tool. Beyond that lie your own code with SQL and Spark APIs and open-source libraries such as dlt (data load tool), Airbyte or Debezium. The deciding factors are source support, who maintains the code, and support expectations. A proprietary mainframe protocol with no ready-made option ends at a custom connector or DIY code.

concepts.heading: Semi-Structured Data: VARIANT, JSON Strings, STRUCT, MAP
concepts.body: Semi-structured data has four main storage patterns. A JSON string keeps a complete raw copy with no type information and no pre-processing, but the whole string is parsed on every query, so reads are slowest. VARIANT stores JSON in an optimized binary encoding that outperforms JSON strings, copes with new fields and changed types, and is the form Databricks recommends over JSON strings. STRUCT gives the best read performance for a well-known schema, but types are enforced on write, so it needs pre-processing and suits fewer columns. MAP and ARRAY keep typed keys and values without statistics and balance around 500 fields. Example: events from many producers with hundreds of fields that change type and are queried selectively fit VARIANT, created with `parse_json(payload)` and read with `v:user.id::int`. For a STRING holding JSON, `raw:store.bicycle.price` extracts a field as a string, and `::double` casts it, which matters for sorting because strings sort as text. `from_json(col, 'id INT, geo STRUCT<lat: DOUBLE, lon: DOUBLE>')` turns a string into a typed struct.

concepts.heading: Safe Casting and Limits of VARIANT
concepts.body: Dirty values are common in semi-structured sources. `variant_get(v, '$.price', 'double')` extracts and casts a field but the query fails if a value such as n/a cannot be cast, while `try_variant_get` takes the same arguments and returns NULL, which keeps the job running. The same idea appears elsewhere: `try_cast` and `try_to_timestamp` return NULL instead of failing. `schema_of_variant` shows the schema found across rows, and conflicting types fall back to VARIANT. Keep the original value in bronze so rejected values can be inspected later. VARIANT has limits: it cannot be used as a clustering key, partition column or Z-order key, and it cannot be compared, grouped, ordered or used in set operations. When a field is filtered, joined or clustered on constantly, promote it to a typed top-level column derived at write time and keep VARIANT for the long tail, as in `CREATE TABLE events (customer_id BIGINT, v VARIANT) CLUSTER BY (customer_id)`. Struct fields, unlike variant fields, can be clustering keys and collect statistics.

concepts.heading: Unstructured Files and Domain 2 Consolidation
concepts.body: Unstructured data such as images, scanned PDFs and audio is stored in Unity Catalog volumes or cloud object storage. Auto Loader supports the binaryFile format, which reads each file into one row with path, modificationTime, length and content (bytes) columns: `spark.readStream.format('cloudFiles').option('cloudFiles.format','binaryFile').load('/Volumes/main/docs/scans')`. Writing those rows to Delta gives governed, incremental tracking, and later jobs can parse files or run models on the table. To consolidate Domain 2 (about a fifth of the exam), run a mental decision chain. How fresh must data be, and is it new files, a table, a database, a SaaS app or a bus? Pick incremental batch with availableNow when hours are acceptable. Prefer streaming tables or Auto Loader for files, managed connectors for supported databases and SaaS, partitioned JDBC or REST code when nothing else fits, and federation when copying is not wanted. Then decide how the schema may change: enforce, evolve, or rescue.

examPoints: A question that weighs copying data against querying it in place, or a one-off small file against a pipeline, is testing the recommendation to ingest for repeated heavy use, Lakehouse Federation for read-only occasional access, and file upload for tiny one-time loads.

A question about flexible JSON with many changing fields and good read speed is testing VARIANT, while a failing cast on a mixed-type field is testing try_variant_get and a field used as clustering key is testing promotion to a typed column.

A question on PDFs or images landing in a volume is testing Auto Loader with the binaryFile format, and a source with no managed connector is testing community, custom or partner options in that order.

quiz.q: A bronze table receives telemetry JSON from 40 firmware versions. Fields appear and change type with new releases, there are several hundred fields, and analysts query only a handful of them. The team wants no pre-processing and good read performance. Which column design fits best?
choices: A STRING column holding the raw JSON, parsed by `raw:path` on each query, because strings never fail on type changes
A STRUCT column with all several hundred fields declared, because structs enforce types and give the best performance at any width
A MAP column of STRING to STRING, because maps store statistics for every key and keep the cost of reads low
A VARIANT column, because it stores JSON in an optimized binary form and tolerates new fields and changed types
quiz.explain: VARIANT is the recommended type for flexible semi-structured data, faster to read than JSON strings and tolerant of drift. A STRUCT needs types fixed at write time and degrades with hundreds of columns; MAP and ARRAY keep no statistics.

quiz.q: A department wants a Unity Catalog table from a vendor-supplied PostgreSQL system for an occasional, exploratory review. The vendor forbids copies of its data for now, and analysts must be granted access table by table. Which approach fits the stated needs?
choices: A scheduled managed connector with a gateway, because it copies the tables incrementally into streaming tables
A partitioned JDBC read in a nightly Lakeflow Jobs notebook that writes the tables into a bronze schema
A Lakehouse Federation foreign catalog, which queries the source read-only and is governed per table in Unity Catalog
A file upload of exported tables, because uploads create tables without any connection to the source database
quiz.explain: Federation queries the source in place, read-only, with Unity Catalog table-level control, so no copy is made. The managed connector, the nightly JDBC read and the upload all create copies, which the vendor forbids.

days.recap: Ingest for repeated heavy use, federate for occasional read-only access, upload for tiny one-offs, and walk down managed, community, custom, partner, DIY. Semi-structured: VARIANT over JSON strings, STRUCT for stable schemas, try_variant_get for dirty values, promote hot fields. Unstructured files use Auto Loader binaryFile.

days.title: Bronze to Silver: Tolerant Casting, NULL Handling, Quarantine, Joins and Unions

concepts.heading: Casting and Parsing Dirty Text
concepts.body: Bronze keeps raw, often all-string data; silver keeps typed, trustworthy data. A strict `CAST(quantity AS INT)` raises CAST_INVALID_INPUT when it meets N/A or 12x and the whole query fails, which is right when bad data must stop a pipeline but wrong for a tolerant cleaning step. `try_cast(quantity AS INT)` returns NULL instead, so the job converts what it can and keeps NULL for the rest; comparing with the raw column then reveals the rejected rows: `SELECT order_id, try_cast(quantity AS INT) AS quantity, quantity AS quantity_raw FROM bronze.orders`. Dates work the same way: `to_timestamp(s, fmt)` may raise an error, `try_to_timestamp(s, fmt)` returns NULL, and the format is a real pattern, not a hint. For mixed formats, `coalesce(try_to_timestamp(ts,'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss'), try_to_timestamp(ts,'MM/dd/yyyy'))` takes the first that parses and leaves the rest NULL. Text such as `$1,234.50` needs symbols removed first: `CAST(regexp_replace(price,'[$,]','') AS DECIMAL(12,2))`. Use DECIMAL for money because DOUBLE is binary floating point and can introduce rounding errors in sums.

concepts.heading: NULL Handling and Three-Valued Logic
concepts.body: Missing data needs a decision per column: keep NULL, replace it with a default, or reject the row. `coalesce(country, 'UNKNOWN')` returns the first non-NULL argument and supplies a default. The look-alike `nullif(a, b)` does the opposite job, returning NULL when a equals b, so it turns placeholders into NULL: `nullif(trim(email), '')` first trims spaces and then maps empty text to a real NULL, which makes `IS NULL` and `COUNT(email)` behave correctly. The trap is SQL's three-valued logic. Any ordinary comparison with a NULL side is unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true, so `WHERE status <> 'CLOSED'` silently drops tickets with no status. Fix it with `status IS DISTINCT FROM 'CLOSED'`, which treats NULL as a comparable value, or with `coalesce(status,'') <> 'CLOSED'`. The null-safe equality `a <=> b` (same as `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`) is true when both sides are equal or both are NULL. In PySpark, `df.dropna(subset=['order_id','customer_id'])` drops a row when any listed column is NULL, whereas without subset every column is examined and `fillna` replaces instead of removing.

concepts.heading: Quarantine Instead of Silent Drops
concepts.body: Dropping bad rows is the simplest cleaning step but it loses information about why data was rejected, and it fails a rule such as no record may silently disappear. The quarantine pattern splits a batch with a validity flag: valid rows go to the silver table, invalid rows go to a quarantine or rejected table with a column that holds the failure reason, so people can review them, correct them and run them through the same logic again. In PySpark, add a flag with `withColumn('is_valid', F.col('amount') >= 0)`, write `filter('is_valid')` to silver and `filter('NOT is_valid')` to the quarantine table. Both writes should append. The same design suits tolerant casting: rows where try_cast produced NULL from a non-NULL source value are the candidates for quarantine. Note the layering: bronze stays raw and untouched so that any rule can be fixed and replayed; silver is where you type, trim, standardize, deduplicate and validate; the quarantine table is the audit trail between them. Later in Domain 3, expectations in Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines formalize the same idea.

concepts.heading: Joins: Choosing the Type and Avoiding Row Explosions
concepts.body: With orders as the left table and customers as the right, INNER keeps only matches, LEFT keeps every order and fills customer columns with NULL when no match exists, LEFT SEMI keeps orders that have a match and never repeats a row, LEFT ANTI keeps orders without a match, and CROSS returns every combination. Semi and anti joins return only left columns, so they replace EXISTS and NOT EXISTS filters; the orphan list for a data steward is a left anti join. A cross join on purpose builds a scaffold, 300 stores by 12 months gives 3,600 rows, so a later left join does not lose empty months, but a join with no condition is treated as a cross join, a frequent cause of surprise growth. If a join key is only part of the right side's key, each left row matches many rows and sums are overstated: join on every key column, `ON s.store_id = p.store_id AND s.sku = p.sku`, and compare count(*) before and after. NULL never equals NULL with `=`, so use `<=>` when NULL keys should pair up. In PySpark, `join(df, 'customer_id')` returns the key once, while an expression condition keeps two columns and a later reference is ambiguous.

concepts.heading: Unions, Broadcast and Stream-Static Joins
concepts.body: UNION ALL appends rows and keeps duplicates; UNION also removes duplicates, which costs a shuffle and an aggregation over all columns, so use UNION ALL when the inputs are disjoint, such as two regional tables with distinct orders. INTERSECT and EXCEPT are the set operators for rows in both inputs or only in the first. In PySpark `union` lines up columns by position, so a different column order silently mixes values and may even succeed after type widening; `unionByName` matches by name. When one side lacks a column, `unionByName(df_new, allowMissingColumns=True)` fills NULL, and in SQL you add `CAST(NULL AS STRING) AS channel` to the older query. For performance, a broadcast hash join copies a small table to every executor so the large table is not shuffled: `tx.join(broadcast(codes), 'currency')` or the hint `/*+ BROADCAST(t) */`. Hints are suggestions that Spark may ignore, and only the small side should be broadcast. When a stream must be enriched from a small, slowly changing Delta table, a stream-static join is stateless, joining each micro-batch with the current version of the static table, while a stream-stream join keeps state and needs watermarks.

examPoints: A question where a cleaning job fails on bad text or must keep running with unparseable values as NULL is testing try_cast and try_to_timestamp, with coalesce for defaults and nullif for placeholders.
A question where rows with missing values vanish from a filter, or NULL keys fail to match in a join, is testing three-valued logic and the null-safe operators IS DISTINCT FROM and <=>.
A question on joins and unions is testing the right type (left, anti, semi, cross), a complete composite key, UNION ALL for disjoint data, unionByName by name, and broadcast of the small side.

quiz.q: A silver build filters bronze with `WHERE channel NOT IN ('test','internal')`. A support lead reports that rows whose channel is NULL are missing, but they must be kept as normal customer traffic. Which condition keeps them while still excluding the two channels?
choices: Replace NOT IN by `<> 'test' AND <> 'internal'`, which treats NULL as a value different from both literals
Add `OR channel = NULL` to the condition, because equality with the NULL literal is true for missing values
Wrap the column in `try_cast(channel AS STRING)`, which turns every NULL into an empty string before the comparison
Use `coalesce(channel, '') NOT IN ('test','internal')`, so NULL rows become a comparable value and stay
quiz.explain: A comparison with NULL is unknown and WHERE drops unknown rows, so the NULLs must be turned into a comparable value, for example with coalesce, or compared null-safely. Splitting NOT IN into <> conditions still yields unknown, and = NULL is never true.

quiz.q: A job combines yesterday's `df_a` with columns (id, region, amount) and today's `df_b` whose columns arrive as (id, amount, region, channel). The new column channel must appear with NULL for older rows and values must be matched by column name. Which call does this?
choices: df_a.unionByName(df_b, allowMissingColumns=True), which matches by name and fills the missing channel with NULL
df_a.union(df_b), because union aligns columns by name and adds channel automatically for missing columns
df_a.join(df_b, 'id', 'left'), which stacks the rows of both frames and fills channel for the older ones
df_b.unionByName(df_a), because unionByName without extra options adds missing columns on its own
quiz.explain: unionByName matches by name and, with allowMissingColumns=True, fills columns missing on one side with NULL. Plain union is positional and fails on a different column count, and a join combines columns rather than stacking rows.

days.recap: Silver is typed and trustworthy: try_cast and try_to_timestamp tolerate dirty text, coalesce and nullif handle missing values, three-valued logic needs IS DISTINCT FROM or <=>, and a quarantine table keeps rejects. Pick joins by intent (left, anti, semi, cross), join on the full key, use UNION ALL and unionByName, and broadcast the small side.

days.title: Reshaping Columns and Rows: explode, split, Renaming, Deduplication and Aggregates

concepts.heading: Arrays to Rows: explode, explode_outer and posexplode
concepts.body: Silver tables are usually flat, but bronze data often carries arrays. `explode(array)` creates one output row per element, and for a NULL or empty array it creates no row at all, so the parent record silently disappears. `explode_outer` behaves the same but returns one row with a NULL element for a NULL or empty array, so the parent survives. `posexplode` adds the zero-based position as a column named pos next to the element (col), which is the safe way to keep the order of an ordered list, because Spark does not guarantee row order after a shuffle. For an array of structs, `inline` expands each struct into columns. A MAP exploded gives key and value columns. Example: `SELECT order_id, explode_outer(items) AS item FROM bronze.orders` keeps orders that have no items. PySpark has the same functions in F.explode and F.explode_outer. When a question says every parent row must still appear, the answer is the outer variant.

concepts.heading: split Takes a Regex and Struct Fields Use Dot Notation
concepts.body: `split(str, regex [, limit])` cuts a string around matches of a regular expression and returns an array. Because the delimiter is a regex, special characters such as the pipe, dot, parenthesis and plus need escaping: `F.split("addr", "|")` uses an empty alternative and cuts between every character, while `F.split("addr", r"\|")` or `"[|]"` splits on a literal pipe. Elements are read by zero-based index with `parts[0]` or one-based with `element_at(parts, 1)`. A limit of -1 or zero means no cap on the number of pieces. For STRUCT columns no split is needed: fields are read with dot notation (`address.city`), and `address.*` expands every field into a top-level column, so fields added to the struct later flow through. Summary of types: STRUCT to columns with `.*`, ARRAY to rows with explode or inline, STRING to ARRAY with split, MAP to rows with explode. Pick the function by the source type.

concepts.heading: Renaming and Dropping Columns
concepts.body: There are two meanings of rename. `withColumnRenamed` or an alias changes the name only in that DataFrame or query result; the stored table is untouched until you write it out. Renaming a column of a Delta table in place needs column mapping: `ALTER TABLE silver.events SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.columnMapping.mode' = 'name')` and then `ALTER TABLE silver.events RENAME COLUMN usr_id TO user_id`. With column mapping the table maps logical names to physical Parquet names kept in metadata, so renaming or dropping is a metadata-only change and the data files are not rewritten. Name mode can be enabled on an existing table, while id mode only at creation, and enabling it raises the table protocol, so check that every reader supports it first. A CTAS copy also works but rewrites all the data. To leave columns out of a projection, `SELECT * EXCEPT (ssn, birth_date)` keeps all the others and automatically includes columns added to the source later; in PySpark use `df.drop(...)`. Do not confuse it with the EXCEPT set operator, which compares rows.

concepts.heading: Deduplication: dropDuplicates, row_number and QUALIFY
concepts.body: `SELECT DISTINCT` and `dropDuplicates(["customer_id"])` remove rows that repeat on the listed columns, but when two rows share the key and differ in other columns, Spark keeps whichever it meets first, and after a shuffle that order is not guaranteed. So the result can change between runs. When you need the latest row per key, number the rows within each key with a window function and keep the first one: `SELECT * FROM customer_updates QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1`. `QUALIFY` filters on a window function result without a subquery. Before choosing a strategy, find the problem keys with `GROUP BY invoice_id HAVING count(*) > 1`: WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot test an aggregate, HAVING filters the groups. For a stream, deduplication needs state, so use `withWatermark` plus `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"])`, with a delay longer than the largest gap between copies. Note that PRIMARY KEY in Unity Catalog is informational and does not stop duplicates.

concepts.heading: Aggregates, NULL and Approximate Counts
concepts.body: Most aggregates skip NULL inputs. `count(*)` counts all rows, `count(expr)` counts rows where expr is not NULL, and `count(DISTINCT expr)` counts different non-NULL values. With 1,000 rows, 200 NULL emails and 600 different addresses among the rest, the three give 1000, 800 and 600. `avg(rating)` divides the sum of non-NULL ratings by the number of non-NULL ratings; a group with only NULLs returns NULL. Replacing NULL with `coalesce(rating, 0)` turns missing values into real zeros and lowers the average, so only do it when the business meaning is zero. An exact `count(DISTINCT x)` must keep every distinct value, which gets heavy on billions of rows. `approx_count_distinct(x[, relativeSD])` uses HyperLogLog++ with a small fixed sketch and a default maximum relative standard deviation of 5%; use it for dashboards and monitoring, and keep exact counts for billing and reconciliation. For profiling, `df.describe()` gives count, mean, stddev, min, max, and `df.summary()` adds approximate percentiles (25%, 50%, 75% by default).

examPoints: A question that needs every order to stay in the output even when its array is empty or NULL is testing explode_outer, because explode drops those parents.
A question about the latest record per key being different on each run is testing row_number() with QUALIFY or a window, not dropDuplicates, which keeps an arbitrary row.
A question about count results with NULLs or a faster unique count is testing count(*) versus count(col) versus count(DISTINCT col), and approx_count_distinct when a small error is acceptable.

quiz.q: A silver job reads a bronze table with a column `tags` of type ARRAY<STRING>. Some rows have tags NULL, and analysts report that a count of orders in silver is lower than in bronze after the job runs SELECT order_id, explode(tags) AS tag. Which change keeps every order in silver?
choices: Replace explode with posexplode so the position column prevents any orders from being removed from silver
Replace explode with explode_outer so orders with a NULL or empty array produce one row with a NULL tag
Wrap the call in size(tags) so that orders with no tags get a count of zero and an extra row is added
Add DISTINCT to the select so Spark restores the rows that were lost earlier during the explode step
quiz.explain: explode emits nothing for a NULL or empty array, so the parent row vanishes; explode_outer emits one row with a NULL element. posexplode only adds an index and still drops those orders, and DISTINCT cannot bring back rows that were never produced.

quiz.q: A table `readings` has several rows per `sensor_id` with a `ts` column. A nightly job runs df.dropDuplicates(["sensor_id"]) to keep the newest reading, but the retained row differs between runs. Which statement explains it and gives the fix?
choices: dropDuplicates always keeps the oldest row, so ordering by ts ascending before the call guarantees the newest is kept
The column ts has a different type in each partition, so casting sensor_id to string before the call fixes the order
dropDuplicates compares all columns by default, so passing the list of keys turns off the random choice of the row that is kept
dropDuplicates keeps an arbitrary row after a shuffle; use row_number() over sensor_id ordered by ts descending, keep row 1
quiz.explain: With key columns specified, Spark keeps an arbitrary one of the matching rows depending on partition order. A window with row_number and an ORDER BY makes the choice explicit. Sorting beforehand does not guarantee which row survives after the shuffle.

days.recap: Explode drops empty parents unless you use explode_outer; split is a regex; EXCEPT/drop remove columns and column mapping renames a Delta column without a rewrite; use row_number with QUALIFY for the latest row per key; count(col) skips NULLs and approx_count_distinct trades accuracy for speed.

days.title: Tuning Spark on Databricks: Shuffle Partitions, Parallelism, Memory, Broadcast Joins and AQE

concepts.heading: Shuffle Partitions Decide Task Size
concepts.body: A shuffle, caused by groupBy, joins and distinct, redistributes rows into a fixed number of partitions and each partition becomes one task. `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` sets that number for DataFrame and SQL queries; the documented default is 200 and the value `auto` lets Databricks pick from the query plan and input size. Too few partitions means each task is big, memory runs out and tasks spill to disk. Too many means a swarm of tiny tasks with scheduling overhead and small output files. Example: a groupBy over 600 GB with 200 shuffle tasks gives several GB per task and heavy spill in the Spark UI, so raising the setting (for example to 2000, or auto) cuts the size of each task. Adaptive query execution can coalesce small partitions after the shuffle, but it does not add partitions for an oversized aggregation (it splits only skewed join partitions), so the starting number still matters for big data. You set it in the notebook with `SET spark.sql.shuffle.partitions = 2000` or in the compute Spark config.

concepts.heading: Parallelism: Two Settings, Two APIs
concepts.body: Spark has two similarly named partition settings, and exam questions test which one applies. `spark.default.parallelism` is the default number of partitions for RDD transformations such as join, reduceByKey and parallelize when the code gives no number; DataFrame and SQL work does not read it. `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` controls the partitions after a shuffle in DataFrame and SQL queries. Since modern Databricks code is written with DataFrames and SQL, the second is the one to tune. Example: a developer sets `spark.default.parallelism 800` in the cluster Spark config and then runs a pure SQL GROUP BY; the Spark UI still shows 200 shuffle tasks, because the SQL query never reads the RDD setting. Reading input also has its own partitioning, which is separate from shuffle partitions. The rule of thumb is to identify the API in the stem first, then choose the setting that belongs to it.

concepts.heading: Broadcast Joins and the Threshold
concepts.body: In a broadcast hash join Spark sends a copy of the small side to every executor and joins the large side in place, so the large table is not shuffled. Spark picks it automatically when the estimated size of one side is below `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold`. A hint such as `SELECT /*+ BROADCAST(dim) */ ...` forces it regardless of the threshold, but changes the query text. Example: a 20 GB fact table joined with a 150 MB dimension shows a sort merge join with a full shuffle in the plan; raising the threshold above 150 MB, or hinting the dimension, gives a broadcast join and removes the shuffle of the 20 GB side. The cost is memory: the broadcast table is collected on the driver and held on each executor, so a threshold that is too high causes out-of-memory errors. Accurate table statistics matter, because the decision uses estimated size. Adaptive query execution can also convert a sort merge join into a broadcast join at runtime, using its own adaptive threshold, when the real size turns out small.

concepts.heading: Memory: Driver, Executors and Spill
concepts.body: The driver runs the notebook code and coordinates executors; `collect()` brings every row into the driver process, so the whole result must fit in driver memory and more executors do not help. Avoid collect on large data, write the result to a table or keep processing in Spark, and if the data must reach the driver choose a larger driver node type, which can be set separately from the workers. On the executor side, memory comes from the worker instance type. More memory per core means less spill to disk. Databricks guidance says not to hardcode properties such as `spark.executor.memory` or `spark.dynamicAllocation.*` in compute or job definitions, because hardcoded values override built-in optimizations and often waste money or reduce performance. To give tasks more memory, pick a memory-optimized instance family or an instance with fewer cores per GB, or reduce the data per task with more shuffle partitions. Serverless compute manages these settings for you, which is why only a limited set of Spark properties can be configured there.

concepts.heading: Adaptive Query Execution and Measuring Changes
concepts.body: Adaptive query execution (AQE) is on by default and re-optimizes a query using statistics collected at runtime. It coalesces small shuffle partitions, switches join strategies (for example to broadcast) and handles skewed joins by splitting large partitions, so on current Databricks compute the first tuning step is usually to leave AQE on and fix the data layout or the starting partition count, not to disable features. Tuning claims need evidence. A single faster run proves little because settings interact with data volume, skew, cluster size and caching. Compare with the same input or date range, change one parameter at a time, and look at stage durations, shuffle read and write sizes, spill, and task counts in the Spark UI, repeating when run times vary. Example: changing shuffle partitions from 200 to 2000 and seeing 40 minutes drop to 31 looks good, but if the fast run read less data the gain may come from the input. A setting that helps a large shuffle can hurt many small jobs with tiny tasks, so do not roll it out to every job on one measurement.

examPoints: A question about heavy spill with few huge shuffle tasks is testing spark.sql.shuffle.partitions (more partitions, or auto), not executor count or an RDD setting.
A question where spark.default.parallelism changes nothing for SQL is testing that it applies to RDD operations while DataFrame and SQL shuffles use spark.sql.shuffle.partitions.
A question about a performance claim from one run is testing controlled measurement: same input, one change at a time, compare Spark UI metrics; also do not hardcode executor memory.

quiz.q: A nightly aggregation runs on classic compute with the default shuffle settings. The Spark UI shows a shuffle stage with 200 tasks that each read about 4 GB and spill to disk, while most cores of the cluster sit idle. Which change addresses the cause?
choices: Increase spark.default.parallelism because the aggregation is written as a SQL GROUP BY
Raise spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold so that the aggregation is broadcast to the executors
Increase spark.sql.shuffle.partitions so the shuffle is split into more and smaller tasks
Use collect() on the aggregated result so that the driver finishes the spilled work in memory
quiz.explain: Too few shuffle partitions create oversized tasks that spill, and idle cores show that more tasks can run at once. default.parallelism is read only by RDD code, the broadcast threshold concerns joins, and collect would push the data to the driver.

quiz.q: A query joins a 30 GB orders table with a 90 MB currencies table. The plan shows a sort merge join, table statistics are current, and the join is slow because of the shuffle of orders. The cluster has plenty of memory. What is the most appropriate fix?
choices: Broadcast currencies with a BROADCAST hint or a higher threshold so that orders is not shuffled
Increase spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to 20000 so that the shuffle of orders becomes much cheaper per row
Set spark.executor.memory in the job definition to force Spark to keep the orders table in memory
Convert the join to a cross join so that Spark no longer has to compare join keys during the join
quiz.explain: A table of 90 MB is small enough to copy to each executor, which removes the shuffle of the large side. More shuffle partitions still shuffle every row, hardcoded memory conflicts with Databricks guidance, and a cross join multiplies rows instead of reducing work.

days.recap: Spill with giant shuffle tasks means raise spark.sql.shuffle.partitions (or auto); default.parallelism is for RDDs; broadcast small tables, mind the memory risk; collect needs a bigger driver, not more executors; leave AQE on, do not hardcode executor memory, and re-measure with the same input.

days.title: Gold Layer Objects and Data Quality: Materialized Views, Views, Streaming Tables, Constraints and Expectations

concepts.heading: Choosing the Gold Object
concepts.body: Gold objects serve consumers, so the choice depends on cost, freshness and who writes. A table stores data that jobs write and maintain with INSERT, MERGE, UPDATE and DELETE. A view stores only its query; each access recomputes against current sources, which suits cheap logic such as a column projection or simple filter, and always-current data. A materialized view stores the precomputed result as a Unity Catalog managed table and updates it when refreshed, often incrementally, so it fits joins and aggregations read by many people, for example a dashboard over hundreds of millions of rows. A streaming table processes each record of an append-only source once and fits ingestion and row-level incremental logic, not recomputed aggregates. Example: a regional sales summary built from a join and aggregation over large silver tables and opened all day by fifty analysts is a materialized view, because the work is paid once per refresh instead of once per click. Note that old names appear in documents: pipelines were called Delta Live Tables.

concepts.heading: Streaming Tables Versus Materialized Views
concepts.body: The difference that exam questions probe is what happens when old data would change. A streaming table reads each source row once. If it joins a stream with a dimension, the result is fixed when the row was processed, and later changes in the dimension do not update rows already written. That is useful for point-in-time history and for row-by-row enrichment of append-only events, but is described in the docs as potentially fast but wrong if you need current values. A materialized view is correct as of its last refresh: when the dimension changes, Databricks recomputes the affected parts of the result, incrementally when it can. Example: customers move to new segments every week and revenue per segment must always reflect the current segment, even for past orders; that is a materialized view. A clickstream where each event gets a few derived columns once is a streaming table. A streaming table is owned by one pipeline, and no other pipeline can change a table that a pipeline defines.

concepts.heading: Refreshing Materialized Views and Who Writes a Table
concepts.body: A materialized view shows the data of its last refresh, so a refresh must be triggered. You can run `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW name` manually, define a schedule in the view (`SCHEDULE CRON '0 30 3 * * ?' AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'` or `SCHEDULE EVERY`), or add a Lakeflow Jobs task right after the upstream load so that the refresh follows the data: a SQL task running the REFRESH statement for a standalone view, or a pipeline task when the view is defined in a pipeline. If analysts see yesterday's numbers after the nightly load, the usual cause is that nothing refreshed the view. You cannot add rows to it with INSERT because the contents come from the query. When several processes must write, correct or delete rows with custom MERGE logic, the right gold object is a regular Delta table, which any job or user with privileges can modify, and BI tools read it like any table. A view stores no data at all, so there is nothing to refresh, only a query to run each time. Decide by who owns the writes, how often the data is read and how fresh it must be.

concepts.heading: Enforced and Informational Constraints on Delta Tables
concepts.body: Delta tables enforce two constraint types: NOT NULL on a column and CHECK with a boolean expression. A write that violates either fails and the transaction is rolled back. `ALTER TABLE main.silver.payments ADD CONSTRAINT positive_amount CHECK (amount > 0)` first verifies that all existing rows satisfy the rule; if one row violates it, the statement fails and nothing is added, so fix or quarantine the bad rows and rerun. PRIMARY KEY and FOREIGN KEY in Unity Catalog are informational: they document relationships and can help the optimizer, but Databricks does not check them, so an insert of a duplicate key succeeds. To guarantee unique keys, deduplicate before writing with row_number and QUALIFY or a MERGE on the key, or schedule a check that finds duplicates. Constraints apply to every writer of the table, which makes them the right tool for rules that must never be broken, while expectations in pipelines add metrics and flexible actions for pipeline datasets.

concepts.heading: Expectations in Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines
concepts.body: An expectation is a named SQL boolean condition on a dataset of a pipeline (streaming table, materialized view or view) plus an action for violating records. The default `EXPECT` (Python `expect`) warns: invalid rows are written and the metrics count them. `ON VIOLATION DROP ROW` (`expect_or_drop`) removes invalid rows before the write and logs only the count of dropped records. `ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE` (`expect_or_fail`) makes the update fail, and for table updates the transaction is rolled back so the previous result remains; a person must fix code or data and rerun. Choose by impact: warn when bad rows are tolerable, drop when they can be excluded safely, fail when wrong data is unacceptable, as for a finance report. The constraint cannot hold custom Python functions, external service calls or subqueries on other tables, so a referential check is written as a join in the query and a simple flag column. Dropped rows are not stored anywhere; if the business must review them, use a quarantine dataset built with the negated rule next to the clean one.

examPoints: A question about a heavily read aggregate over large tables is testing a materialized view, while an always-current projection with no extra storage is a view and custom MERGE writers need a Delta table.
A question where a dimension changes after rows were processed is testing that a streaming table keeps the value from processing time while a materialized view recomputes.
A question about bad rows is testing expectation actions (warn, drop, fail) and quarantine for review; PRIMARY KEY is informational while NOT NULL and CHECK are enforced.

quiz.q: A pipeline loads card transactions into a silver streaming table. About 2% of rows have a NULL merchant_id. Fraud analysts must be able to inspect these rows later, while the clean table must not contain them and the pipeline must keep running. Which design fits?
choices: Use ON VIOLATION DROP ROW only, because Databricks keeps the dropped rows in the event log for later review by analysts
Use ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE so that every NULL stops the update until the fraud analysts correct all the rows
Use a plain EXPECT without an action, because warned rows are automatically moved into a separate review table
Expect-or-drop on merchant_id IS NOT NULL for the clean table, plus a second dataset using the negated rule as quarantine
quiz.explain: Drop removes invalid rows and logs only a count, so a second dataset built with the negated rule keeps the rows for review. Fail would stop the pipeline, and a plain EXPECT writes the invalid rows into the target without moving them anywhere.

quiz.q: A data team writes a gold object that sums revenue per day from silver sales tables with 2 billion rows. Executives query it all day, and a figure that is one hour old is acceptable. They also want to avoid recomputing the sum for each query. Which object should they create?
choices: A standard view over the silver tables, because the query result is cached permanently after the first call
A materialized view refreshed on a schedule, so the aggregate is stored and updated, often incrementally
A streaming table with a MERGE statement run by several jobs, so each job can correct the totals
A Delta table with an informational PRIMARY KEY on the day column to make the aggregate unique
quiz.explain: A materialized view stores the precomputed result and refreshes it, which matches the accepted lag and avoids recomputation. A view recomputes on every access, a streaming table is owned by one pipeline and suited to row-level logic, and an informational key does not compute anything.

days.recap: Gold choice: materialized view for stored aggregates and joins, view for cheap always-current logic, streaming table for append-only row processing, Delta table when many writers use MERGE; NOT NULL and CHECK are enforced, keys are informational; expectations warn, drop (count only) or fail, and a quarantine dataset keeps bad rows.

days.title: Lakeflow Jobs Reliability and Control Flow: Retries, Run if, If/else, For each and Task Types

concepts.heading: Retries and Timeouts
concepts.body: In Lakeflow Jobs (formerly Workflows) each task has advanced settings with a retry policy: how many times a failed task run is retried and how long to wait between attempts. For most configurations the default is no retry, so a transient error fails the run at once. The retry applies only to that task and the rest of the job graph is untouched, and the interval is measured from the start of the failed attempt to the start of the next one. Retries suit transient problems such as network resets or a briefly unavailable source; they do not fix logic errors, since the same code fails the same way. A timeout is the maximum duration of a task run; when exceeded, the status becomes Timed Out. When both are set, the timeout applies to each attempt separately. A task with a 30-minute timeout and 2 retries can therefore run as three attempts, so the worst case is attempts times timeout plus waiting. If a hard overall limit matters, lower the timeout or the retry count. A continuous job has its own handling: exponential backoff after repeated failures.

concepts.heading: Run if: Reacting to Upstream Outcomes
concepts.body: By default a task runs only when all its dependencies succeeded (All succeeded). If a dependency fails, the task is marked Upstream failed and does not run. The Run if setting changes this, based on the tasks in Depends on. Options: All succeeded (default), At least one succeeded, None failed (none failed and at least one ran), All done (run after every dependency finished, whatever the outcome), At least one failed and All failed (run only for failure cases; otherwise the task is Excluded, i.e. skipped). Example: a cleanup task that must release a lock row after ingest, transform and report, whether or not they succeeded, uses All done and lists every task that could leave the lock. An alert task that must fire when any of four parallel loads fails, and be skipped otherwise, uses At least one failed, because All failed would wait for every load to fail. Also consider the siblings: if b and c both depend on a and b fails, c still runs, but d depending on both with the default setting becomes Upstream failed.

concepts.heading: Conditions and Loops: If/else and For each
concepts.body: The If/else condition task evaluates a boolean expression of two operands and an operator. Operands can be job parameters, task parameters or task values set upstream with `dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key="bad_records", value=n)` and referenced as `{{tasks.count_rows.values.bad_records}}`. Downstream tasks choose a branch in Depends on, `check (true)` or `check (false)`, and the other branch is not run.
