The operators differ: `==` and `!=` compare as strings, so `12.0 == 12` is false, while `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=` compare numerically. A For each task runs one nested task once per element of an input array, which can be a JSON array, a task value or a job parameter. Inside, `{{input}}` is the element, or `{{input.table}}` for an object field. Concurrency sets how many iterations run in parallel and defaults to 1, so raise it for parallel work. The nested task can be any standard type except another For each. Example: 40 table names from a control table feed a For each running one notebook, with concurrency 8.

concepts.heading: Task Types and Dependencies
concepts.body: A job is a directed acyclic graph of tasks, and a task starts when its own dependencies are met, with as many tasks in parallel as possible. Task types match the work. A SQL task runs a saved query or a .sql file with several statements (from the workspace or a Git provider) on a serverless or pro SQL warehouse, not on a job cluster; use a notebook task when Python or Spark code is needed. A Dashboard task refreshes a published dashboard after the data it shows has been rebuilt. A pipeline task starts an update of a Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines pipeline and, in a triggered job, ends when the update completes; it has an optional full refresh setting. A Run Job task runs another job in the same workspace as a step and can pass job parameters; circular calls and nesting beyond three Run Job tasks are not supported. A For each task is one node: downstream tasks depend on the For each task, not the nested task, and use All done if they must run even when some iterations fail.

concepts.heading: Repair Runs, Idempotency and Disabling Tasks
concepts.body: A repair run re-runs only the unsuccessful tasks of a multi-task run and the tasks that depend on them; successful tasks are not run again, which saves time and compute. Failed tasks use the current job and task settings, so you can fix a notebook path or cluster setting first. The catch: a repaired task starts from its first line, and Lakeflow Jobs does not make tasks idempotent. If the task appended a million rows with INSERT INTO before failing, the repair appends them again and the table holds duplicates. Retries carry the same risk. Idempotent writes produce the same end state when run twice: `MERGE INTO ... ON key`, `INSERT OVERWRITE` of a partition, or `replaceWhere`. Disabling a task skips it at run time and keeps its configuration and history, which is useful when a task is broken while the rest of the job keeps running. Downstream tasks are then evaluated by their Run if condition, and an If/else or For each task fails if the task providing its input is disabled. To skip a task for one run only, use Run now with different settings.

examPoints: A question about a transient network failure is testing the task retry policy, and about a timeout combined with retries it is testing that the timeout applies to each attempt.
A question about a task that must run whatever happened upstream, or only after a failure, is testing Run if (All done, At least one failed); If/else compares with == as strings.
A question about repeating a notebook for many inputs is testing For each with concurrency, and a failed multi-task run is testing repair run, with idempotent writes to avoid duplicates.

quiz.q: A job has three load tasks that run in parallel and a task named notify_owner that sends a message. The message must be sent as soon as any one of the loads has failed, and it must not run when all loads succeeded. Which Run if setting should notify_owner use, with all three loads as dependencies?
choices: All failed, so it runs when each of the three loads has failed and is excluded otherwise
None failed, so it runs when no dependency failed and at least one of them has run
At least one failed, so it runs when one or more dependencies failed and is excluded otherwise
All succeeded, because a task with that setting reports the failure status of its dependencies
quiz.explain: At least one failed matches a partial failure and skips the task when everything succeeded. All failed would stay silent if only one load fails, None failed is the opposite condition, and All succeeded never runs after a failure.

quiz.q: A transform task in a three-task job appends rows to a Delta table with INSERT INTO and then fails in a later step. After a repair run, the task succeeds, but the table contains the appended rows twice. What is the best way to prevent this in the future?
choices: Make the write idempotent, for example MERGE INTO on a key or INSERT OVERWRITE of the partition
Increase the retry interval so the second attempt starts after the first commit is cleaned up
Disable the task before repairing so Lakeflow Jobs removes its earlier output automatically
Set Run if to All done on the transform task so that the earlier rows are ignored by the repair
quiz.explain: A repair or retry starts the task from the beginning, and rows already committed stay. Writing in a way that gives the same end state when repeated avoids duplicates. Waiting longer, disabling or changing Run if do not remove rows that were already written.

days.recap: Retries are per task and fit transient errors, with the timeout applied per attempt; Run if (All done, At least one failed) steers on outcomes; If/else compares == as strings; For each needs concurrency above 1 for parallelism; repair reruns only failed and dependent tasks from the start, so writes must be idempotent.

days.title: Schedules and Triggers: Scheduled, File Arrival, Table Update, Continuous, Time-Based or Data-Driven

concepts.heading: Scheduled Triggers, Time Zones and Skipped Runs
concepts.body: The scheduled trigger starts a job on a time basis. A simple schedule runs periodically at a chosen unit and interval and you cannot set the time of the first run. An advanced schedule lets you pick the period, the start time and a time zone and shows the Quartz cron expression: `0 15 2 * * ?` is 02:15:00 every day. Choose the time zone with care: with a zone that observes daylight saving time, an hourly job is skipped or appears delayed by an hour or two when DST begins or ends, and choosing UTC gives every hour in absolute time. A job also has a maximum number of concurrent runs, by default 1. When a trigger fires while the limit is reached, the new run does not start and is recorded as Skipped (queueing is a separate job setting). Example: a job scheduled every 15 minutes whose run once takes 40 minutes leaves skipped runs in the history, visible in the runs list and the matrix view, instead of a pile-up of overlapping runs.

concepts.heading: File Arrival Triggers
concepts.body: A file arrival trigger starts a run when new files land in a Unity Catalog volume or external location. It monitors the root or a subpath and checks recursively, so a trigger on `/Volumes/main/landing/raw/` also sees `region=eu/` and deeper folders. The path cannot contain wildcards such as `*` or `?`, and it must not include external tables or managed locations of catalogs and schemas. Only new files start runs, with a best-effort check roughly every minute. A file replaced under the same name is not a new file and does not start a run, so producers should write uniquely named, immutable files, for example with a timestamp in the name. The trigger only says that something new exists; it does not remember what was processed. Pair it with Auto Loader in the notebook: `spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles")...trigger(availableNow=True)` with a checkpoint reads exactly the files that arrived since the last run, even when runs were skipped or delayed. Keep the checkpoint outside the monitored location so its files do not start new runs.

concepts.heading: Table Update Triggers
concepts.body: A table update trigger starts a job when monitored tables change: managed Delta and Iceberg tables, external Delta tables, materialized views, streaming tables, and views that depend on them. Updates include inserts, updates, merges and deletes. The trigger reads table metadata and history as the job's Run as principal, which needs SELECT on every monitored table plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA. After the Run as identity changed to a new service principal without SELECT, the job simply stops starting, and failure notifications also cover a trigger that cannot evaluate. With several tables choose Any table is updated or All tables are updated; a report that joins two tables refreshed by separate pipelines at different times needs All. Dynamic value references pass context into parameters, for example `{{job.trigger.table_update.updated_tables}}` as a JSON list of the tables changed since the last run. A trigger on a view does not evaluate the view's filter: it considers the view updated whenever a dependent table changes. Views using read_files, non-Unity-Catalog tables or federated tables are not supported.

concepts.heading: Cooldown Versus Debounce, and Continuous Jobs
concepts.body: File arrival and table update triggers share two rate controls. Minimum time between triggers is a cooldown: at most one run per interval, and after a run completes the trigger waits that long before starting another. Wait after last change is a debounce: the trigger waits after the most recent arrival before starting, and each new file or commit resets the timer. For batches, pick a debounce longer than the gap inside a batch and shorter than the gap between batches: 300 files land within 40 seconds and the next batch is 50 minutes away, so 60 seconds starts one run per batch. The same fixes the table case where an upstream pipeline writes with three MERGE statements a few seconds apart and the job starts on the first one. If small files arrive every few seconds all day, a debounce never fires because the timer keeps resetting; use the cooldown. For always-on streaming, a continuous job is recommended: one active run, restarted when it ends or fails, normally within about a minute, with exponential backoff after repeated failures. The scheduler is not meant for low-latency work.

concepts.heading: Choosing Time-Based or Data-Driven
concepts.body: Pick the trigger from the requirement. Use a scheduled trigger when the clock defines the need, such as a dashboard due at 06:00 by compliance, when inputs are reliably ready earlier: with upstream loads finishing by 04:30, a 05:00 schedule leaves a margin, whereas a data trigger would give no assurance if data never arrives and the job would not run at all. Use a data-driven trigger when the start should follow the data or arrivals are irregular: a vendor dropping files zero to eight times a day suits a file arrival trigger, which runs only when a new file exists, combined with Auto Loader and availableNow. Two separately owned jobs whose finishing time varies between 01:30 and 04:00 suit a table update trigger on the downstream job, not a guessed schedule. If producer and consumer belong to one job, use task dependencies instead. Data-driven triggers need something in Databricks to watch; a REST API with no notification and nothing written to a volume or table must be started on a schedule or by an external orchestrator calling the Jobs API. Sensor events needed within seconds point to a continuous job.

examPoints: A question about a missing hourly run near a clock change is testing DST in the schedule's time zone; choose UTC for absolute hours, and slow runs with one concurrent run end up Skipped.
A question about irregular file drops or two jobs where finishing time varies is testing the file arrival or table update trigger, usually with Auto Loader availableNow, over a guessed schedule.
A question about starting once after a batch is testing Wait after last change (debounce), while continuous arrivals are tested by Minimum time between triggers (cooldown).

quiz.q: A partner uploads about 500 files to a Unity Catalog volume every night between 01:00 and 03:00, with new files arriving every few seconds in that window. The ingestion job should run once after the upload has finished and not start repeatedly during it. Which configuration fits?
choices: A file arrival trigger on the volume path with Minimum time between triggers set to one second
A simple schedule every hour, because file arrival triggers cannot detect more than one file
A file arrival trigger on the volume path with Wait after last change set to a few minutes
A continuous job that restarts as soon as the previous run ends so each file is processed at once
quiz.explain: A debounce longer than the gap between files in the batch waits for the upload to settle and starts one run. A tiny cooldown would still start many runs, hourly schedules ignore when the data is ready, and a continuous job would run all day for a nightly upload.

quiz.q: A team monitors the Unity Catalog table main.sales.orders with a table update trigger. After the job's Run as identity was changed to a new service principal, the job stops starting although the table is updated every hour and no error appears in the run list. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The table update trigger can only run as the user who created the job, and service principals are unsupported
The new service principal lacks SELECT on the table, so the trigger cannot read its history and evaluate it
Table update triggers stop after the first change, so they have to be recreated after each update
The cooldown of the trigger is counted in days after an identity change, which suppresses the run
quiz.explain: The trigger reads table metadata as the Run as principal and needs SELECT plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA. Without them the trigger cannot evaluate and the job does not start; failure notifications can reveal it. The other statements are not documented behavior.

days.recap: Scheduled triggers follow the clock (DST can skip hourly runs, UTC avoids it; busy jobs are Skipped); file arrival watches a volume path without wildcards and needs new unique files; table update needs SELECT for Run as; debounce for batches, cooldown for steady streams; data-driven when arrivals vary, scheduled when a deadline matters, continuous for seconds-level streaming.

days.title: Development Workflow: Databricks Git Folders, Bundle Variables and Target Overrides

concepts.heading: The Git Folder Development Flow
concepts.body: Databricks Git folders (formerly Repos) are embedded Git clients in the workspace. Each team member clones the repository into a personal Git folder, for example under `/Workspace/Users/<you>/`, creates a feature branch, edits notebooks and files, commits and pushes, then opens a pull request on the Git provider and merges it after review. Merge conflicts are resolved in the Git folders UI, and pulling brings others' work into your folder. A Git folder is a local checkout with one current branch. If several people share one folder and one of them switches the branch, notebooks change for everyone, which is why the guidance is that only one user performs Git operations on each Git folder. The fix for such surprises is a personal Git folder per engineer; a collaborator can use Share to copy a link that opens a dialog pre-filled with the folder's configuration. When the default branch is protected and you cannot commit there, create a new branch from the Git dialog, push, open a pull request in the Git provider and pull the merged result back.

concepts.heading: Production Git Folders and Large Repositories
concepts.body: A production Git folder differs from a user-level development folder. It is created by an admin outside user folders on a deployment branch such as release, users get run-only access (Can Run), and only admins and a service principal used by automation may update it. It is updated only by automation when a pull request is merged, for example external CI/CD such as GitHub Actions calling the Repos API, or a scheduled job that pulls. Jobs then run the reviewed code and developers cannot edit it in the workspace. Databricks recommends Declarative Automation Bundles for packaging and deploying CI/CD; the production Git folder is the option when you only deploy code. Git folders have memory and disk limits per operation, so a very large repository can fail to clone with a size error, and Databricks recommends against creating Git folders from monorepos. Use sparse checkout mode, which clones only chosen directories with a cone pattern when you create the folder, or remove large files from history with a tool such as git filter-repo (requires a force push) or split the code into separate repositories.

concepts.heading: Bundles and Variables
concepts.body: A bundle, now called Declarative Automation Bundles (formerly Databricks Asset Bundles), describes jobs, pipelines and other resources in YAML next to the code, so the same files can be deployed to several environments. Environment differences go in the targets mapping. Declare a custom variable under `variables:` with an optional default and description, reference it anywhere as `${var.<name>}`, and give target-specific values under `targets.<target>.variables`. Example: `variables: {schema_name: {default: etl_dev}}` and in the prod target `variables: {schema_name: etl_prod}` give one job definition for both environments. Substitutions such as `${bundle.target}` build names from the current target. A variable can also use a lookup that finds an object's ID by name when the bundle is deployed, for example `warehouse_id: {lookup: {warehouse: "Shared Analytics"}}`, so no workspace-specific ID appears in the files. Lookups exist for object types such as cluster, cluster_policy, job, pipeline, service_principal and warehouse. Variables are resolved at deploy time.

concepts.heading: Variable Precedence and Deployment-Time Values
concepts.body: When a variable could get a value from several places, the CLI looks in this order and stops at the first one it finds: the `--var` option of the bundle command, environment variables starting with `BUNDLE_VAR_`, the file `.databricks/bundle/<target>/variable-overrides.json`, the `variables` mapping within targets, and finally the default in the top-level definition. Command line beats environment, which beats files, target values and defaults. This lets CI pass a one-time value without editing YAML. If a variable has no default and no source gives a value, you must supply one. Bundle variables are deployment-time: the CLI interprets them in `bundle deploy`. Running a job runs the already deployed definition, so passing a different bundle variable when starting the job from the Jobs UI has no effect. For values that change on every run, define job parameters or task parameters and pass them at run time. Use the same way of setting variables for deploy and run commands, so they refer to the same deployment.

concepts.heading: Target Overrides Merge by Key
concepts.body: Settings in a target are merged with the top-level settings, and where the same setting appears in both, the target wins. Items in lists are matched by key, so only the changed fields need repeating: job clusters are matched by `job_cluster_key`, job tasks by `task_key` and pipeline clusters by `label`. Example: a top-level job has a job cluster with `job_cluster_key: main` and 2 workers; the prod target contains `resources: jobs: my_job: job_clusters: - job_cluster_key: main new_cluster: num_workers: 8`. Prod then uses 8 workers on the same cluster while the spark_version and every other setting come from the top-level definition. Copying the whole job into the target is therefore unnecessary, and a second copy of the job definition would be harder to maintain. Together with variables, overrides keep one definition of the pipeline logic while dev, test and prod differ only in the few settings that must differ, such as the schema name, the workspace host or the cluster size.

examPoints: A question about several engineers working on the same repository is testing one personal Git folder per person with feature branches and pull requests; a shared folder with a switched branch changes code for everyone.
A question about code that only automation updates and users run is testing the production Git folder (Can Run, deployment branch), with bundles as the recommended CI/CD route.

A question about environment-specific values is testing bundle variables, targets overrides and lookups; the --var option beats environment variables, files, target values and defaults, and run-time changes need job parameters.

quiz.q: A bundle defines a job with a task whose cluster is declared at the top level with `job_cluster_key: etl` and 4 workers. The prod target needs 16 workers on that cluster, and every other setting must stay the same. The team wants to avoid duplicating the job. What should they write?
choices: A second job with a different name in the prod target, copying all tasks and the cluster with 16 workers
A bundle variable passed to the job at run time from the Jobs UI so that prod picks up 16 workers
A change to the top-level job to 16 workers, because targets cannot override settings of top-level resources
In targets.prod, override the job's job_clusters entry with job_cluster_key: etl and num_workers: 16
quiz.explain: Target settings merge with the top-level ones, and job clusters are matched by job_cluster_key, so only the changed field is repeated. A copied job duplicates the definition, bundle variables are not changed at run time, and targets can override top-level settings.

quiz.q: A bundle declares `variables: {batch_date: {default: '2026-01-01'}}`. The prod target sets batch_date to '2026-06-01' under its variables, and the environment of the CI runner contains BUNDLE_VAR_batch_date=2026-09-01. The pipeline runs databricks bundle deploy -t prod --var batch_date=2026-10-01. Which value does the deployment use?
choices: 2026-10-01, because the --var option has the highest precedence
2026-09-01, because environment variables beat command-line options
2026-06-01, because the target value always wins over any external input
2026-01-01, because the top-level default is the only value used at deploy time
quiz.explain: The order is --var, then BUNDLE_VAR_ environment variables, then the variable-overrides file, then the target's variables, then the default. The command-line value is found first, so the other three sources are ignored.

days.recap: One personal Git folder per engineer, feature branch, pull request; production Git folder is run-only and updated by automation; bundles use variables with ${var.name}, lookups for IDs, and targets that merge by key (job_cluster_key, task_key, label); precedence is --var, BUNDLE_VAR_, overrides file, target, default; bundle variables are deploy-time only.

days.title: Deploying Bundles: Targets, Modes, run_as, Binding and the Databricks CLI

concepts.heading: Targets and Deployment Is Declarative
concepts.body: A bundle's targets mapping defines deployment destinations, each with its own workspace host, mode, variables and run_as. The same source files and resources are deployed to each. `databricks bundle deploy -t test` deploys to the named target; without `-t` the default target is used. A common flow is validate, deploy to dev or test, run integration tests, then deploy to prod with the same bundle. Bundles track the resources they create in a state stored in the workspace. On each deploy, a resource in the configuration but not in the workspace is created, a resource in both is updated, and a resource that was deployed before and is no longer in the configuration is removed. So deleting a job from the YAML and deploying deletes it in the workspace. The YAML is the source of truth, manual changes in the workspace can be overwritten, and the `lifecycle` setting can protect critical resources from being destroyed. Resources are matched by IDs in the state, not by names.

concepts.heading: Development and Production Modes
concepts.body: Setting `mode: development` on a target applies defaults for pre-production work. Resources that are not files or notebooks get the prefix `[dev <short_name>]` and jobs and pipelines get a dev tag; Lakeflow pipelines are marked development true; schedules and triggers are paused (set `pause_status: UNPAUSED` on a specific schedule to run it); concurrent runs are enabled and the deployment lock disabled; and `--cluster-id` can override compute definitions on deploy. That explains why a developer finds the scheduled job not running and prefixed names. `mode: production` instead validates settings and does not allow overriding cluster definitions. It checks that pipelines are development false, that the current Git branch equals the optional `git.branch` of the target (`--force` overrides this check), and it recommends service principals through run_as; without them it checks that paths are not overridden to a user and that run_as and permissions are specified. Deploying to a mode: production target with git.branch main from a feature branch therefore fails. In CI/CD, production deployments normally run from the main branch after review.

concepts.heading: Run Identity and Bundle Identity
concepts.body: The `run_as` setting, at the top level or within a target, defines the identity used to run bundle jobs and pipelines: a user_name or a service_principal_name. Non-admins can only set it to themselves. For production the recommended pattern is a service principal, so workflows are not tied to a person's account: if the engineer who deployed leaves, jobs that ran as that person lose permissions. The deploying identity needs permission to use the service principal, and the principal can have fewer permissions than the deployer. Different targets can use different identities, for example dev as a user and test and prod as service principals. A bundle's identity comes from its root_path, by default `~/.bundle/${bundle.name}/${bundle.target}` in the deployer's home. So two engineers deploying the same bundle to the same target each get a separate copy of the jobs. Changing the bundle name, target or workspace makes the bundle forget the association. To share one deployment, use a shared root_path, such as a service principal's or a common folder, normally deployed by CI.

concepts.heading: Databricks CLI Commands: validate, plan, deploy, run, destroy
concepts.body: The bundle commands of the Databricks CLI map to the lifecycle. `databricks bundle validate` checks that the configuration files are syntactically correct, prints a summary of identity (name, target, workspace host, user, path) and warns about properties that are not in the schema; it is the usual first step in CI. `databricks bundle plan` shows the actions a deploy would take on each resource, such as create jobs.my_bundle_job, without changing anything, so reviewers can see the effect of a pull request. `databricks bundle deploy` deploys to a target. `databricks bundle run KEY` runs a job or pipeline, and `--only task_a,task_b` runs specific tasks, with a `+` prefix adding upstream tasks and a `+` suffix adding downstream ones: `+clean` runs ingest and clean, `clean+` runs clean and publish. `databricks bundle summary` prints identity and deployed resources with links. `databricks bundle destroy` permanently deletes the jobs, pipelines and artifacts deployed by the bundle; it asks for confirmation unless `--auto-approve`, and it must run with the original name, target and workspace.

concepts.heading: Deploy Options and Adopting Existing Resources
concepts.body: Deploy flags cover CI needs. `--auto-approve` skips interactive approvals, which non-interactive CI needs. `--fail-on-active-runs` fails the deployment if jobs or pipelines in it are running, which protects a long-running production job from an update in the middle of a run. `--force` overrides validations such as the Git branch check, `--force-lock` forces acquiring the deployment lock, and `-c, --cluster-id` overrides the cluster in development. A frequent trap involves existing resources. `databricks bundle generate job` writes configuration for a job that already exists, but deploying that YAML creates a second job and leaves the original unmanaged. `databricks bundle deployment bind KEY RESOURCE_ID` links the bundle resource to the existing workspace resource, which then becomes managed by the bundle and is updated by the next deploy; bind does not recreate data, so pipeline data and materialized views remain. Use `--target`, or add `--bind` to generate. `unbind` reverses the link and deletes nothing.

examPoints: A question about jobs paused and prefixed after a deploy is testing mode: development, while a production deploy that fails from a feature branch is testing mode: production with git.branch (override with --force).
A question about jobs failing when the deploying engineer leaves is testing run_as a service principal in production; two copies of a bundle point to root_path and identity.
A question about previews, partial runs or adopting a resource is testing bundle plan, bundle run --only with +, and bundle deployment bind; destroy deletes what the bundle deployed.

quiz.q: An engineer ran databricks bundle generate job against a production job that was created manually, committed the YAML and deployed the bundle to prod. The workspace now has two jobs with the same tasks, and only the new one is managed by the bundle. Which step should have been taken so that the deployment updates the existing job?
choices: Run databricks bundle destroy first so that the manual job is deleted and the YAML takes its place
Run databricks bundle deployment bind with the job key and the ID of the existing job, then deploy
Run databricks bundle validate with --force so that the CLI links resources with equal names
Set mode: development on the target so that Databricks merges duplicate jobs into one job
quiz.explain: Resources are matched by IDs in state, not by names; bind links the YAML resource to the existing job, which is then updated on deploy. Destroy only removes what the bundle deployed, validate does not link anything, and development mode adds prefixes instead of merging.

quiz.q: A release engineer wants a review step in CI that lists which jobs and pipelines of a bundle would be created, updated or deleted by the next deployment to prod, without changing the workspace or running anything. Which command provides this?
choices: databricks bundle destroy -t prod --auto-approve
databricks bundle run -t prod --only +publish
databricks bundle plan -t prod
databricks bundle deployment unbind -t prod
quiz.explain: bundle plan builds the bundle and prints the actions per resource without changing the workspace. Destroy deletes deployed resources, run starts tasks, and unbind removes a link to an existing resource.

days.recap: Targets deploy the same bundle to dev, test and prod, and YAML is the source of truth (removed resources are deleted on deploy); development mode prefixes and pauses, production mode validates branch and run_as; use a service principal for run_as; CLI: validate, plan, deploy, run (--only, +), destroy; bind adopts existing resources.

days.title: Monitoring Jobs: Run History, Statuses and Failure Trends

concepts.heading: The Runs tab as a performance baseline
concepts.body: Every job has a Runs tab with a matrix view and a list view. In the matrix, the Run total duration row shows one bar per run. The bar color gives the state: green for succeeded, red for unsuccessful, pink for skipped, yellow for waiting for retry, grey for pending, canceled or timed out. The bar height gives the duration. The Tasks rows below show one cell per task and run, so one slow task stands out from the rest. Hovering over a bar shows start time, duration, cluster and status. This view is the first place to look when nobody reports a failure but the job feels slower. A staircase of taller bars over several weeks is a regression trend, for example because the input table keeps growing. One tall bar among normal ones is an outlier, for example a cluster that started slowly. For example, a nightly job that used to take 20 minutes and now takes 35 shows a rising staircase in the Run total duration row, and the task rows tell you which task grew.

concepts.heading: Graph, Timeline and List views of one run
concepts.body: A single run has its own details page with three views. Graph shows the DAG of tasks with their status, and clicking a task shows its cluster, source code, start and end time, duration and status. Timeline shows each task as a bar on a time axis, so you can see which tasks took long, how tasks overlapped and which dependencies held others back. List shows one row per task with status, name, type, duration and dependencies, and can be filtered and sorted by status, name or duration. A task starts only when its upstream tasks are done, so a run can only be as fast as its slowest upstream chain. In the timeline, a long bar followed by many tasks that all start exactly when it ends marks the blocker. For example, a 12-task job that took two hours instead of 50 minutes with no failure is best diagnosed in the Timeline view: find the long bar, then open that task to see its cluster and code. Use the Graph view for logic and the Timeline for time.

concepts.heading: How a run status is decided: leaf tasks
concepts.body: Databricks derives the status of a run from its leaf tasks, the tasks that no other task depends on. Succeeded means all tasks were successful. Failed means one or more leaf tasks failed. Succeeded with failures means some tasks failed but all leaf tasks were successful. Skipped, Timed Out and Canceled describe runs that did not start, ran over their time limit or were stopped. A task that never ran because its upstream failed did not succeed, so it counts against the run if it is a leaf. For example, take extract, transform and load in a chain, plus a side task notify that depends on extract. If transform fails, load is never executed. The leaves are load and notify. Notify succeeded, but load did not, so the whole run is Failed even though one leaf is green. Remember the rule as: look at the ends of the graph, not at the middle. A failed task in the middle does not by itself make a run red when every leaf finishes successfully.

concepts.heading: Succeeded with failures and notifications
concepts.body: Because the status follows the leaves, a failed task that is not a leaf can leave the run as Succeeded with failures. This happens when the downstream leaf has a Run if condition such as All done, so it runs anyway. Databricks treats Succeeded with failures as a successful state for notifications. Job notifications can be sent for Start, Success, Failure, Duration warning and Streaming backlog events, to email addresses or to system destinations such as Slack or a webhook. The Failure event fires when a run ends in an unsuccessful state. A notification that is set for Failure only therefore stays silent for a Succeeded with failures run. To hear about such a run, subscribe to the Success event too; the message carries the run link, and the failed task can then be found in the Graph or List view. For example, a nightly job has an optional enrichment task that fails twice a week. Nobody gets a failure email, yet data is incomplete. The fix is the Success notification plus a check of the task graph, not a retry setting.

concepts.heading: System tables and the workspace Runs tab
concepts.body: The Jobs UI keeps run history only for a limited time (about two months), and Databricks recommends exporting results before they expire. For longer periods and for questions across all jobs, query the jobs system tables in the system.lakeflow schema: jobs, job_tasks, job_run_timeline and job_task_run_timeline. The timeline tables slice long runs into hourly rows with period_start_time and period_end_time, so one run can span several rows. The result_state and termination_code columns are filled only in the row where the run ends, so counting outcomes needs `WHERE result_state IS NOT NULL`. A daily failure rate is `count_if(result_state IN ('FAILED','ERROR')) / count(*)` over those rows, grouped by date. To compare this month with the same month last year, sum the period durations per job and compare. For a quick workspace-wide look, the Runs tab under Jobs and Pipelines lists runs of all jobs and pipelines you can access, with filters for status, run-as user and error code. Its Finished runs count graph and Top 5 error types table answer the question of what failed most this week.

examPoints: Run status comes from leaf tasks: any failed or unrun leaf makes the run Failed, while a failed non-leaf with all leaves green gives Succeeded with failures.
A Failure-only notification stays silent for Succeeded with failures; add the Success event to be told.
Use the Runs tab matrix for trends and the system.lakeflow tables, filtering result_state IS NOT NULL, for long history and account-wide failure rates.

quiz.q: A nightly Lakeflow Jobs job has the tasks ingest, clean and publish in a chain, and a leaf task audit_log that depends on ingest. In one run clean fails. ingest and audit_log succeed. What status does the run get?
choices: Succeeded with failures, because the job's first task and the audit_log leaf both finished successfully
Failed, because publish never ran after clean failed, so one leaf task did not succeed
Succeeded, because only tasks that actually started are counted when the run status is derived
Skipped, because publish did not start and the run therefore counts as not executed
quiz.explain: The leaves are publish and audit_log. Publish never ran because its upstream clean failed, so a leaf did not succeed and the run is Failed. Succeeded with failures needs all leaf tasks to be successful.

quiz.q: A platform team needs the count of failed runs per job for the last 90 days, from a SQL notebook, covering jobs of the whole account. Runs longer than an hour must not be double counted. Which approach fits?
choices: Read the Finished runs count graph on the Runs tab and note the failed bars for each job over the period
Open the matrix view of each job in the workspace and count the red bars in the Run total duration row by hand
Query system.lakeflow.job_run_timeline and count every row whose period_start_time falls in the last 90 days
Query system.lakeflow.job_run_timeline, filter result_state IS NOT NULL, and count FAILED and ERROR per job_id
quiz.explain: Timeline rows are hourly slices; result_state is set only on the row where the run ends, so filtering on it gives one row per finished run, and FAILED and ERROR both mark an unsuccessful run. Counting all rows would double count long runs, and the UI views cover limited history and one job at a time.

days.recap: Run status follows the leaf tasks. Succeeded with failures counts as success for notifications. Use matrix and Timeline for trends and blockers, and system.lakeflow tables (result_state IS NOT NULL) for long history across jobs.

days.title: Reading the Spark UI: Skew, Shuffle and Spill

concepts.heading: Stages, tasks and the stage page
concepts.body: Spark splits a job into stages, and each stage into tasks, one task per partition. A stage is finished only when its slowest task is finished, so the slowest task sets the stage time. The stage page in the Spark UI has a Summary Metrics table that shows the distribution of task durations as minimum, 25th percentile, median, 75th percentile and maximum. It also shows the I/O columns Input, Output, Shuffle Read and Shuffle Write, and the spill statistics when the stage spilled. Reading the UI is a way of measuring before you change anything. First find the longest stage, then ask which of three patterns it shows: skew when a few tasks run far longer than the rest, spill when data went from memory to disk, or an I/O or shuffle bottleneck when a large volume moves. For example, a join-and-aggregate job has one stage of 40 minutes while the others take minutes. Open that stage and compare the maximum and the 75th percentile of the task durations before choosing any fix.

concepts.heading: Skew: one partition much larger than the rest
concepts.body: Skew means a few partitions hold much more data than the others, usually because a few key values dominate a join or group-by. Those tasks run long while the other cores sit idle, which wastes the cluster and stretches the job. Databricks gives a rule of thumb: if the maximum task duration is about 50% or more above the 75th percentile, the stage probably has skew. In a healthy stage the two numbers are close. Typical fixes depend on the cause. Adaptive query execution (AQE) can split skewed partitions in sort merge joins. Salting the hot keys, or aggregating in two stages, spreads a dominating key across tasks. Clustering the source table helps when the skew comes from the stored layout. A REBALANCE hint helps when the stage writes a table. Adding more workers does not help much, because the single large partition is still processed by one task. For example, a stage where the median task is 20 seconds and the maximum is 12 minutes is a clear case, and more nodes would leave the 12-minute task unchanged.

concepts.heading: Spill: memory pressure
concepts.body: Spark uses execution memory for shuffles, joins, sorts and aggregations. When a task needs more than it has, Spark writes intermediate data from memory to local disk and reads it back later. That is spill. It keeps the job alive, but it is expensive. The stage details at the top of the stage page show spill statistics only when the stage spilled, so their absence means no spill. Spill is most common during shuffles. Typical remedies are to use auto-optimized shuffle with spark.sql.shuffle.partitions set to auto, to reduce the data held in memory by selecting fewer columns and rows and avoiding very large string, array, map or struct columns, and to give executors more memory. For complex batch ETL with joins over several tables, use fewer, larger workers: each has more memory per task and less data crosses the network. For streaming queries, limit the batch size so micro-batches do not spill. Note the difference from skew: with spill, task durations can be even, but every task is slow and writes to disk.

concepts.heading: Is the stage bound by input, output or shuffle?
concepts.body: The I/O columns of the stage table tell you where the time goes. A rough rule from the Databricks guide: take the largest value of Input, Output, Shuffle Read and Shuffle Write, divide by the total number of cores and by the stage duration. If the result is about 3 MB per second per core, the stage is probably I/O bound. A large Input means the stage reads a lot of data: store data in Delta, use liquid clustering so selective filters can skip files, make the query more selective, use Photon, use the disk cache for repeated reads, or add compute. A large Output means too much is written: reduce rewrites, for example by optimizing merges and using deletion vectors. A large Shuffle value means data moves between executors: set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to auto. For example, a batch job that filters a big Delta table on store_id and shows a huge Input with almost no shuffle reads far more files than needed. Liquid clustering on store_id lets Spark skip the files whose statistics exclude the filter.

concepts.heading: Shuffle partitions and AQE skew handling
concepts.body: A fixed spark.sql.shuffle.partitions count is a poor fit when input volume changes from day to day. Too few partitions create huge tasks that spill, and too many create thousands of tiny tasks. Setting the value to auto lets Spark choose the partition count from the query plan and the input size, together with AQE, which can coalesce small shuffle partitions at runtime. AQE can also split skewed partitions of sort merge joins and shuffle hash joins. It splits a partition only if it exceeds both thresholds: a factor over the median partition size, spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor, and an absolute size, spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes. If AQE is on and a stage is still skewed, the partitions may be below the thresholds, so lower them. Broadcast joins are never skew-optimized. Salting or two-stage aggregation remains the answer when a few key values hold most of the data. After any change, re-run and compare the stage page numbers, so you know the change helped.

examPoints: A maximum task duration about 50% or more above the 75th percentile in Summary Metrics signals skew; more workers will not fix one huge partition.
Spill (memory written to disk) is treated with spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=auto, fewer columns, and fewer, larger workers with more memory.
If AQE is on but skew remains, the partitions may be below skewedPartitionFactor and skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes; lower them or salt the key.

quiz.q: A daily job joins orders with customers and then aggregates. The stage page of the join shows median task time 18 seconds, 75th percentile 25 seconds and maximum 14 minutes. No spill is reported. A colleague proposes doubling the cluster size. What is the best reading and action?
choices: The stage is I/O bound, so doubling the workers divides the maximum task time by two
The stage is skewed on a few keys; salt the hot keys or pre-aggregate, and check AQE skew thresholds
The stage spilled to disk, so the engineer should raise the shuffle partition count to a fixed high number
The result is normal because task times always vary, so no change to the query is needed
quiz.explain: A maximum far above the 75th percentile, without spill, is the skew pattern. One huge partition is still handled by one task, so more workers do not shorten it. Salting, two-stage aggregation or lowering AQE skew thresholds attack the cause.

quiz.q: A join-heavy ETL job on a cluster of many small workers is slow. The stage page shows spill statistics, task durations are similar across tasks, and the Shuffle Read is large. Which change is most in line with Databricks guidance?
choices: Switch to fewer, larger workers with more memory per task and set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to auto
Add an OPTIMIZE ZORDER step before the job so the files are sorted by the join keys and the tasks become even
Disable adaptive query execution so that Spark stops changing the shuffle partition count while the query is running
Replace the join with collect() on both sides and join the resulting rows in Python code on the driver node
quiz.explain: Spill with even task times is memory pressure, not skew. Larger workers give more memory per task and reduce shuffled data, and auto shuffle partitions sizes tasks from the data. Collecting to the driver risks out-of-memory, and disabling AQE removes helpful tuning.

days.recap: Open the longest stage. Max far above the 75th percentile means skew (salt, AQE thresholds); spill means memory pressure (auto shuffle partitions, larger workers); large Input points to clustering and data skipping. Measure again after each change.

days.title: Liquid Clustering, Predictive Optimization and Cluster Troubleshooting

concepts.heading: Liquid Clustering and changing keys
concepts.body: Liquid Clustering replaces Hive-style partitioning and ZORDER for organizing a Delta table. You choose clustering keys with CLUSTER BY, and Spark organizes files by those keys so selective filters can skip files whose min and max statistics rule them out. Unlike partitioning, you can redefine the keys later with ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (...) without rewriting the table. The catch is that the ALTER only changes metadata. Existing files keep their old layout, and a normal OPTIMIZE is incremental: it rewrites only what is needed to cluster new data. To recluster all existing data under the new keys, run `OPTIMIZE events FULL;`. On a large table that was not clustered on the new keys, this can take hours, so plan it. Clustering is not compatible with ZORDER on the same table. For example, a 5 TB events table clustered by customer_id is now filtered mostly by event_date and country. After ALTER TABLE events CLUSTER BY (event_date, country), old data stays slow until OPTIMIZE FULL has run; new writes follow the new keys.

concepts.heading: Automatic Liquid Clustering
concepts.body: Instead of choosing keys by hand, you can let Databricks do it with the CLUSTER BY AUTO clause, either at creation, as in `CREATE TABLE t (a INT, b STRING) CLUSTER BY AUTO`, or on an existing table with `ALTER TABLE t CLUSTER BY AUTO`. Databricks analyzes the historical query workload of the table and picks keys, and changes them when query patterns change. It works on Unity Catalog managed tables and relies on predictive optimization for the key selection and for the clustering work, which run asynchronously. It changes keys only when the predicted savings from better data skipping outweigh the cost of clustering, and it may select no keys at all for small tables or for tables that are not queried often. CLUSTER BY NONE removes the clustering keys. So automatic clustering is the right answer when the access pattern is unknown or changes over time, and fixed keys are the right answer when you know the filters well. If a managed table has CLUSTER BY AUTO but predictive optimization is off, keys will not be adapted.

concepts.heading: Predictive optimization
concepts.body: Predictive optimization automatically runs OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and ANALYZE on Unity Catalog managed tables, using serverless compute for jobs. Databricks identifies the tables that would benefit, queues the work and collects statistics on write, so nobody has to schedule maintenance jobs. For liquid-clustered tables, its OPTIMIZE triggers incremental clustering. It supports only managed tables (Delta and Iceberg): external and foreign tables are not maintained, and ALTER TABLE ... SET MANAGED converts an external Delta table so that Databricks can maintain it. The setting can be enabled at account, catalog, schema or table level, and lower levels inherit from higher ones. You override it with ENABLE, DISABLE or INHERIT, for example `ALTER SCHEMA prod.scratch DISABLE PREDICTIVE OPTIMIZATION`. You need ownership or MANAGE on the object. When predictive optimization is on, a nightly job that runs OPTIMIZE on the same tables only duplicates the work and can be removed. Note that when it runs OPTIMIZE it does not run ZORDER, another reason to prefer liquid clustering. Without it, schedule OPTIMIZE yourself.

concepts.heading: Cluster start failures and init scripts
concepts.body: When a classic cluster does not start, the event log and cluster logs tell you why. An init script is a shell script that runs on every node during startup, before the Spark driver or executor JVM starts. If a cluster-scoped init script returns a non-zero exit code, the launch fails. To troubleshoot, configure cluster log delivery and read the init script log. Databricks recommends compute policies or built-in features instead of init scripts where possible, and installing libraries through policies, not through init scripts. Serverless compute does not support init scripts. A different failure is a cluster that never becomes ready and, after roughly half an hour, ends with a network configuration error and a node daemon ping timeout. The instances started in the customer account but could not reach the Databricks control plane, so check routes, security groups and firewall rules to the control plane, the secure cluster connectivity relay and the storage and token services, for example with `nc -zv host 443`. If the tests pass but a proxy inspects SSL traffic, check the certificates. Distinguish: a script error fails the launch and is read in the init script log, while a network error shows up only after a long wait as a timeout.

concepts.heading: Library conflicts and out-of-memory errors
concepts.body: The %pip magic installs a library into an environment scoped to the notebook session. Other notebooks on the same compute are not affected, and the install does not persist, so it must be repeated in each session; put %pip commands at the top of the notebook. %pip does not restart the Python process by itself. A package that was imported earlier stays in memory, so after `%pip install --upgrade pandas` the old version can still be in use. Call `dbutils.library.restartPython()` after installing, before the rest of the code runs, because it resets Python state. For memory errors, find out which side failed. Actions such as collect() and toPandas() bring the whole result into the driver, so `rows = df.collect()` on a 400 GB table exhausts the driver while executors sit idle. The fix is to do the work in Spark and write the result to a table, or to bring only a small aggregate or sample to the driver. A larger driver helps only with modest results. Executor out-of-memory or spill shows on the stage page and is treated with larger workers or better partitioning.

examPoints: After ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (new keys) old files keep their layout; OPTIMIZE ... FULL reclusters all data.
Predictive optimization maintains Unity Catalog managed tables only; make external tables managed with SET MANAGED, and drop duplicate OPTIMIZE jobs.

A non-zero init script exit code fails the launch; a node daemon ping timeout means a network path to the control plane; %pip needs dbutils.library.restartPython() to load a new version; collect() on a huge table kills the driver.

quiz.q: A team sets `ALTER TABLE clicks CLUSTER BY (country, device)` on a large table that was clustered by user_id. A week later, queries on older months are still slow, while queries on the newest data are fast. What is the most likely explanation and fix?
choices: The ALTER only changed metadata and normal OPTIMIZE is incremental; run OPTIMIZE clicks FULL to recluster existing data
Liquid Clustering cannot change its keys after the table is created, so the table must be rebuilt under a new name
Predictive optimization must be disabled first because it blocks any reclustering of the files written under the old keys
The table needs ZORDER BY (country, device) added next to the clustering keys so that the older months are covered
quiz.explain: Keys can be redefined without a rewrite, but only new data follows them; existing files are reclustered by OPTIMIZE FULL. ZORDER is not compatible with clustering, and predictive optimization does not block the command.

quiz.q: A job cluster fails during startup on every attempt after the team added a cluster-scoped init script that installs an OS package. A different team's new workspace instead waits roughly 25 minutes and then reports a node daemon ping timeout. Which pairing of causes is right?
choices: Both are caused by missing Python libraries, so installing them with %pip on the cluster fixes both of them
The first points to a script exiting with a non-zero code; the second to blocked network access to the control plane
The first points to blocked routes to the control plane; the second points to a script returning a non-zero exit code
Both are caused by driver out-of-memory errors and need a larger driver node type before the clusters can start
quiz.explain: Init scripts run before Spark and a non-zero exit fails the launch quickly; check the init script log. A daemon ping timeout after a long wait means the nodes could not reach the control plane, so routes, security groups and firewall rules must be checked.

days.recap: Changing clustering keys needs OPTIMIZE FULL for old data; CLUSTER BY AUTO and predictive optimization work on managed tables. Init script failure is fast, network timeout is slow. %pip needs restartPython; collect() overloads the driver.

days.title: Managed and External Tables, UNDROP and Conversion

concepts.heading: Managed versus external: who owns the data lifecycle
concepts.body: Both table types are governed by Unity Catalog, which means permissions, lineage and metadata are handled the same way. They differ in who owns the files. A managed table stores its files in the managed storage location of its schema or catalog, and Unity Catalog manages layout, optimization and the file lifecycle. An external table stores its data in a path that you register as a Unity Catalog external location; Unity Catalog manages the metadata but not the lifecycle, optimization, location or layout of the files. Managed tables are the recommended default: storage and maintenance are handled for you, predictive optimization works on them, and they are cheaper to store and to query. Reads and writes to managed tables must use table names, because path-based access is not supported. For example, a team that only queries a sales table from Databricks jobs and dashboards should create it as a managed table. An external table makes sense only when a reason such as outside access to the files exists.

concepts.heading: When to choose an external table
concepts.body: Databricks recommends external tables mainly in two situations. The first is a table over existing data in a format that managed tables do not support, such as JSON or Avro. The second is that non-Databricks clients need direct access to the files and cannot use other access patterns, such as the open Unity APIs with credential vending. External tables can use formats like DELTA, CSV, JSON, AVRO, PARQUET, ORC and TEXT. Keep one trade-off in mind: Unity Catalog privileges are not enforced when outside systems read the files directly, so the security of those files depends on the cloud storage. For example, a feed of Avro files must be queryable in Unity Catalog while a non-Databricks application keeps reading the same files directly. Both conditions point to an external table. If instead the requirement is only to read and write Delta data from Databricks, an external table adds work (you own cleanup and optimization) with no benefit. The choice is about the data's readers and format, not about whether data volume is large.

concepts.heading: Creating an external table: the privileges
concepts.body: An external table must point to a path inside a Unity Catalog external location, which links a cloud storage path with a storage credential. To create one you need CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE on that external location, USE CATALOG on the parent catalog, and USE SCHEMA and CREATE TABLE on the parent schema. The statement is `CREATE TABLE main.finance.audit_ext (id BIGINT) LOCATION 's3://bucket/dir/'`. A managed table needs only the schema-level rights, because Databricks chooses the location. This difference explains a common failure. An engineer holds USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and CREATE TABLE on the schema, runs a CREATE TABLE with a LOCATION clause and gets a permission error. Nothing is wrong with the schema grants; the missing privilege is CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE on the external location. The fix is to have the owner of the location grant that privilege, not to grant more rights on the schema. Remember that the path must be inside a registered external location; a random bucket path will not work.

concepts.heading: Dropping tables, retention and UNDROP
concepts.body: Dropping a table behaves differently by type. Dropping an external table removes only the metadata; the files stay in storage and must be deleted there if they should go. Dropping a managed table removes it, and Databricks keeps the data files for a recovery period, 7 days by default. During that period, `UNDROP TABLE main.sales.daily_totals` brings the table back. After the period an asynchronous purge deletes the files from your cloud storage, and recovery is no longer possible. Dropping a managed table requires MANAGE or ownership, plus USE SCHEMA and USE CATALOG. Do not confuse UNDROP with other commands. RESTORE rolls an existing Delta table back to an earlier version using its history; it cannot revive a dropped table. REFRESH TABLE only invalidates cached metadata and data. For example, if an engineer dropped a managed table by mistake two days ago, UNDROP is the answer; if it was dropped two weeks ago and retention was unchanged, the data is gone, and only a separate backup would help. An external table with a cleanup script that deletes its files is a different risk, because the files belong to you.

concepts.heading: Converting external tables to managed
concepts.body: ALTER TABLE ... SET MANAGED converts an external Delta table into a Unity Catalog managed table. It keeps the table name, settings, permissions, views and history, and it limits downtime: the data is first copied while readers and writers continue, then a short switch moves the final commits and updates the metadata. Path-based reads and writes are redirected afterwards. Requirements are that the table is Delta, that you own it, and that you use supported compute. The syntax depends on the source. External tables use plain `ALTER TABLE t SET MANAGED`; adding MOVE or COPY fails, while foreign tables must specify one of them. CREATE TABLE AS SELECT also converts the data, but creates a new table object and is not recommended against SET MANAGED. Rollback is `ALTER TABLE t UNSET MANAGED`: Databricks keeps the original external data for 14 days, and the command points the table back and preserves the writes made after conversion. Run it before dropping the converted table. To see the type first, use `DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED`, which shows MANAGED or EXTERNAL, the format and the location; SHOW TABLES, DESCRIBE HISTORY and SHOW GRANTS do not show the type.

examPoints: Dropping an external table keeps the files; dropping a managed table keeps them for a recovery period (7 days by default) in which UNDROP TABLE works.
Creating an external table needs CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE on the external location in addition to schema-level rights.
ALTER TABLE ... SET MANAGED converts an external Delta table (no MOVE or COPY); UNSET MANAGED rolls back within 14 days; DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED shows the type.

quiz.q: A table was dropped by mistake nine days ago. It was a managed Unity Catalog table and nobody changed any recovery defaults. The owner needs the data back. What is the correct assessment?
choices: Run UNDROP TABLE, because the default recovery period for dropped managed tables is 30 days after the drop
Run RESTORE TABLE to version 0, which also revives dropped tables by reading them back from Delta history
The default recovery period of 7 days has passed, so UNDROP no longer works and the files may be purged
Run REFRESH TABLE, which re-reads the files from cloud storage and recreates the table definition for you
quiz.explain: The default recovery period after dropping a managed table is 7 days; after that the files are purged asynchronously. RESTORE needs an existing table and REFRESH TABLE only invalidates caches.

quiz.q: An analyst team needs a Delta table in Unity Catalog over data that a non-Databricks tool also writes directly into the cloud storage path. The same team wants Databricks to take over optimization and maintenance for the table later, without changing its name or grants. Which plan matches the facts?
choices: Create a managed table now, because the outside tool can keep writing into its storage path just as before
Create an external table now, then convert it with ALTER TABLE ... SET MANAGED once the outside tool is retired
Create a foreign table now and later run SET MANAGED MOVE so that Databricks takes over the files in place
Create an external table and enable predictive optimization on it, since that also maintains external tables
quiz.explain: Direct file writes by an outside tool are the reason to choose an external table, because path-based access to managed tables is not supported. SET MANAGED later converts it while keeping name, permissions and history. Predictive optimization only maintains managed tables.

days.recap: Managed: Unity Catalog owns files; drop keeps data 7 days, UNDROP works. External: you own files; drop keeps them; creating needs CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE on the location. SET MANAGED converts, UNSET MANAGED rolls back within 14 days.

days.title: GRANT, REVOKE and the Securable Hierarchy

concepts.heading: The hierarchy and the three privileges to read a table
concepts.body: Unity Catalog objects form a hierarchy: the metastore contains catalogs, catalogs contain schemas, and schemas contain tables, views, volumes and functions. Access starts at none. To read a table, a principal needs three things: USE CATALOG on the parent catalog, USE SCHEMA on the parent schema, and SELECT on the table or on a parent that passes it down. USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA let a user navigate into the container but give no data access on their own. Grants go to users, groups or service principals. For example, a BI group analysts that may query only main.sales.orders needs exactly: `GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG main TO analysts`, `GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA main.sales TO analysts` and `GRANT SELECT ON TABLE main.sales.orders TO analysts`. Granting SELECT on the whole catalog would work but breaks least privilege. Granting SELECT alone would fail because the navigation privileges are missing. When a question lists several grant sets, pick the smallest one that contains all three.

concepts.heading: Inheritance: privileges flow downward
concepts.body: A privilege granted on a container is inherited by the objects inside it, both current and future. SELECT on a schema gives SELECT on all current and future tables and views in that schema. SELECT on a catalog applies to all its schemas. Inheritance only goes downward, never up. The scope you grant at is therefore the main design choice. A schema-level grant fits the case of everything in this schema, including tables that will be created later, with no one running a new GRANT. A catalog-level grant is broader than needed if other schemas exist. A table-level grant covers only the named table, so new tables need new grants. There is no wildcard in GRANT object names. For example, data scientists in ds_team need SELECT on every table in main.features, including future ones: `GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA main.features TO ds_team` plus the two navigation privileges. A service principal behind a production pipeline is a grantee in the same way: reference it by its application ID, in backticks, and give it SELECT and MODIFY on the schema when it reads and appends rows.

concepts.heading: REVOKE removes the grant where it was made
concepts.body: REVOKE removes a grant record from the object it names. It does not create an exception on a child object. Consider a group interns that received SELECT on the catalog main. The manager wants interns to lose access to all tables in main.finance but keep the rest. Running REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE main.finance.salaries FROM interns changes nothing, because the access comes from the grant on the catalog, which is still in force and inherited. The fix pattern has three steps. First, revoke at the level of the original grant: `REVOKE SELECT ON CATALOG main FROM interns`. Second, re-grant at a narrower level for what should stay, for example `GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA main.sales TO interns`. Third, check the effective rights with SHOW GRANTS on the catalog and on the schemas. The same logic explains why you cannot carve out an exception with a deny: Unity Catalog access is additive, so the way to remove access is to restructure the grants, or to separate sensitive data into its own catalog or schema.

concepts.heading: Owners, MANAGE and ALL PRIVILEGES
concepts.body: Every securable object has an owner, and owners have all privileges on it, including the right to grant access to others. Privileges can be granted by the object's owner, by the owner of the catalog or schema that contains it, by a user with the MANAGE privilege on the object, or by a metastore admin. So a schema owner can grant on a table inside the schema even when a colleague created the table. MANAGE lets a principal manage privileges, transfer ownership, rename and drop an object. ALL PRIVILEGES grants everything applicable to the object, including what child objects inherit, but it does not include MANAGE, EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA, EXTERNAL USE LOCATION or READ METADATA, to prevent data exfiltration or privilege escalation. For example, a group given ALL PRIVILEGES on a schema can read, write and create tables there, yet fails when it runs a GRANT for others. It needs MANAGE or ownership. Revoking ALL PRIVILEGES leaves MANAGE in place. Prefer group ownership over individual ownership, so access management does not depend on one person leaving the company.

concepts.heading: DENY: what the exam guide lists and what Unity Catalog does
concepts.body: The exam guide names DENY next to GRANT and REVOKE, but you must know where it applies. The SQL DENY statement, which in the legacy Hive metastore takes precedence over any grant and flows down the hierarchy, applies only to hive_metastore and its objects. The reference page states that it is not supported by Unity Catalog. So `DENY SELECT ON TABLE main.hr.salaries TO contractors` is not the way to keep contractors out of HR data in a Unity Catalog table. Do the following instead: do not grant the sensitive objects to those groups, revoke grants they currently hold, and put sensitive data in a separate catalog or schema so that only the groups that need it receive grants. For finer rules, use row filters, column masks or ABAC policies. ABAC DENY policies exist in Unity Catalog, but they are a different mechanism from the SQL statement and are documented as Beta, so do not treat them as the standard answer. On the exam, a Unity Catalog scenario that offers DENY as the fix is usually the distractor; the correct option restructures or revokes grants.

examPoints: Reading a table needs USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT; the first two give navigation only.
Grants are inherited downward; REVOKE works only on the level where the grant exists, so revoke at the catalog and re-grant narrower.
SQL DENY applies only to hive_metastore; in Unity Catalog use REVOKE, restructure grants, or filters, masks and ABAC (DENY policies are Beta). ALL PRIVILEGES excludes MANAGE.

quiz.q: The group `etl_ops` holds SELECT on the catalog `lake`. The security team now wants `etl_ops` to lose access to the schema `lake.hr` but keep access to the other schemas that exist today. Which action achieves this?
choices: Run REVOKE SELECT ON SCHEMA lake.hr FROM etl_ops, which overrides the inherited catalog grant for that one schema
Run DENY SELECT ON SCHEMA lake.hr TO etl_ops, which takes precedence over every grant held in Unity Catalog
Revoke SELECT on the catalog, then grant SELECT on each remaining schema (or move hr into another catalog)
Grant USE SCHEMA to etl_ops on every schema except lake.hr, which removes the inherited reading rights on hr
quiz.explain: A revoke on the schema does not create an exception to a catalog-level grant, and SQL DENY is not supported in Unity Catalog. The grant must be removed where it was made and given again at narrower scopes. USE SCHEMA does not control SELECT.

quiz.q: A new group `quality_leads` must be able to hand out SELECT on the tables of `main.curated` to project teams, without becoming the owner and without being a metastore admin. Which grant fits best?
choices: GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON SCHEMA main.curated TO quality_leads, since it includes every privilege
GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA main.curated TO quality_leads, since holders of SELECT may pass it on
GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA main.curated TO quality_leads, which lets members manage the schema's grants and its objects
GRANT MANAGE ON SCHEMA main.curated TO quality_leads, which allows managing privileges without ownership
quiz.explain: MANAGE lets a principal manage privileges, transfer ownership, rename and drop. ALL PRIVILEGES does not include MANAGE, and SELECT or USE SCHEMA do not allow granting to others.

days.recap: Read a table = USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + SELECT. Grants inherit downward, REVOKE only at the grant level. Owners and MANAGE can grant; ALL PRIVILEGES excludes MANAGE. SQL DENY is hive_metastore-only; ABAC DENY policies are Beta.

days.title: Column Masks, Row Filters and ABAC Policies

concepts.heading: Column masks
concepts.body: A column mask decides what value a user sees in one column. It is a SQL user-defined function registered in Unity Catalog. Its first parameter receives the column value, and it returns either the original value or a masked one; the return type must match, or be castable to, the column type. Each column can have one mask. The table owner, or a user with MANAGE and SELECT, binds it: `ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN ssn SET MASK ssn_mask`, or `ssn STRING MASK ssn_mask` inside CREATE TABLE, and `ALTER COLUMN ssn DROP MASK` removes it. The function often calls is_account_group_member('HumanResourceDept'), so the same query returns the real value for HR and a masked one for everybody else. A mask can use more inputs: further parameters are supplied with USING COLUMNS, which takes other columns of the same table or constants in the order the function expects. For example, `ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN email SET MASK mask_email USING COLUMNS (consent)` shows an email only where consent is true. The data in storage is unchanged; only what the querying user sees is changed.

concepts.heading: Row filters
concepts.body: A row filter is a SQL UDF that returns BOOLEAN and is evaluated for each row at query time. Rows for which it returns TRUE are returned, rows for which it returns FALSE are excluded. Each function parameter is bound to a table column with ON: `ALTER TABLE sales SET ROW FILTER us_filter ON (region)`. Because the function can call identity functions, one filter can give groups different views: `IF(is_account_group_member('admin'), true, region = 'US')` returns every row for admins and only US rows for everyone else. A table can have only one row filter. If two business rules apply, combine them in one function, usually with AND, and keep it short and deterministic, since many conjuncts are harder to optimize. A filter can take several columns, as in `SET ROW FILTER f ON (region, status)`. For a long and fast-changing access list, put the list in a mapping table and let the function look up the user: `RETURN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM valid_users v WHERE v.username = SESSION_USER())`. Then access changes by inserting or deleting rows, not by editing the function.

concepts.heading: Identity functions, requirements and pitfalls
concepts.body: Masks and filters decide per user with identity functions. is_account_group_member('g') is true when the user is a direct or indirect member of the account-level group g; Databricks recommends it for access checks because it tests membership at the account level. is_member('g') also matches workspace-local groups, and the documentation says to prefer the account version. current_user() and session_user() return the user name, not group membership. Attaching a filter or mask is an access-control change, so SELECT is not enough. You need EXECUTE on the function with USE SCHEMA and USE CATALOG on its parents, and for an existing table you must own it or hold both MANAGE and SELECT; creating a table with a filter needs CREATE TABLE on the schema. Pitfalls: the function must be a SQL UDF, so wrap Python logic in a SQL UDF and bind the wrapper. The parameter type must match the column type; with ANSI mode off, a failed implicit cast becomes NULL, and a filter such as d IS NULL then returns every row. CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE keeps an existing row filter, and keeps masks for columns with the same names.

concepts.heading: ABAC: attributes instead of per-table rules
concepts.body: Attribute-based access control (ABAC) in Unity Catalog uses governed tags as attributes and policies that act on everything matching them. Governed tags are account-level tags with built-in rules: creating one also creates a tag policy that fixes the allowed values and says who may assign it. They can be applied to catalogs, schemas, tables and columns, but not to compute resources such as warehouses or jobs. A policy is attached to a catalog, schema or table and is evaluated at query time against all tables below, so tables created later are covered as soon as the right tags are on them. Conditions use has_tag() and has_tag_value(). For example, a team must mask every column holding an email address in about 400 tables across many schemas of prod, and new tables arrive every week: one column mask policy on the catalog, matching columns tagged pii=email, does it, whereas table-level masks would mean 400 manual bindings. Tag inheritance matters: securables inherit governed tags from catalog and schema, but column tags are not inherited from the table. MATCH COLUMNS conditions check column tags only, so tag the columns themselves.

concepts.heading: Writing and operating ABAC policies; GA versus Beta
concepts.body: A policy is created with CREATE POLICY. You need MANAGE on the securable where it is attached, or ownership, and EXECUTE on the UDF (unless the function is inline). TO lists the principals affected, such as account users, and EXCEPT lists exempt principals, who see the original data: `CREATE POLICY mask_ssn_columns ON CATALOG hr COLUMN MASK mask_ssn TO `account users` EXCEPT `compliance team` FOR TABLES MATCH COLUMNS has_tag_value('pii','ssn') AS c ON COLUMN c`. Prefer TO and EXCEPT over group checks inside the UDF. ABAC policies do not show in the table definition; use SHOW POLICIES ON for the object and SHOW EFFECTIVE POLICIES ON to include parent scopes. Table owners cannot override policies set by higher-level admins. Because tags decide which policies apply, restrict who can change them (ASSIGN on the tag, APPLY TAG on the object), audit changes in system.access.audit, and tag new objects with a default restrictive tag. Availability: row filter and column mask policies on tables are the documented core. Metastore-level policies, DENY policies and policies on views are marked Beta, so do not choose them as the standard answer.

examPoints: Column masks and row filters are SQL UDFs; a table has one row filter and a column has one mask; use is_account_group_member, not is_member, for group checks.
Attaching a filter or mask needs ownership or MANAGE + SELECT on the table and EXECUTE on the function; the first mask parameter is the column itself.
One ABAC policy on a catalog (governed tags, TO / EXCEPT) covers many and future tables; column tags do not inherit from the table; metastore-level and DENY policies are Beta.

quiz.q: A `members` table has a STRING column `phone`. Support staff in the account group `support` must see the real number only for rows where the column `opted_in` is true; everybody else sees `***`. Which design is correct?
choices: A row filter on opted_in and the support group, which swaps the phone value for *** in rows that fail the check
A SQL UDF mask_phone(phone, opted_in) that also tests the support group, set with SET MASK ... USING COLUMNS (opted_in)
A Python UDF bound directly as the mask, since Python UDFs are accepted as masks when they are marked deterministic
A dynamic view applied to the table with a row filter, so that the view masks the column for each user
quiz.explain: A mask returns a value per cell, and extra inputs come from USING COLUMNS; the UDF can also test is_account_group_member('support'). Row filters only include or exclude rows, a mask must be a SQL UDF, and row filters or masks cannot be set on a view.

quiz.q: A governance team has one ABAC column mask policy on the catalog `prod` for columns tagged `pii = email`. A new table `prod.crm.leads` is created, but its email column is not masked.
